cards.title: Does general rational linear programming have a strongly polynomial algorithm?
cards.formal: Does there exist a deterministic algorithm, with fixed polynomials p and q, that solves every rational linear program $\min\{c^Tx:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}$, where A has m rows and n columns, using at most p(m+n) elementary arithmetic, comparison, and data-transfer operations, while every intermediate rational number has binary encoding length at most q(N)? Here N is the total input bit length. Solving means returning an exact optimal rational solution if one exists, or correctly reporting infeasibility or an objective unbounded below.
cards.definitions: A is in Q^(m by n), b in Q^m, and c in Q^n, with m,n>=1. All coefficients are supplied explicitly as binary signed numerators and positive denominators. No full-rank, nondegeneracy, strict-feasibility, coefficient-size, or conditioning promise is made. Elementary scalar operations are addition, subtraction, multiplication, division by a nonzero quantity, comparisons, and transfers of stored values. The program is fixed and finite; no oracle, advice, randomization, floor operation, or uncharged access to binary digits is allowed. Rational encoding length means the bit length of a numerator-denominator representation. The polynomial p is independent of N and of every coefficient magnitude; q may depend on N. Consequently the algorithm must also admit a polynomial-time bit implementation. The output is a solution vector, not a required optimal basis. Infeasible means that the feasible set is empty; unbounded means it is nonempty and the infimum of c^T x is minus infinity. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: This isolates whether the combinatorial dimensions of a linear program suffice to control its arithmetic complexity. A resolution would clarify the relation between numerical precision, polyhedral structure, and the complexity of one of optimization’s basic models.

importance.reason: A leading open question in optimization, separating ordinary polynomial-time solvability from a dimension-only arithmetic bound. Its reach includes general linear programming and many combinatorial optimization problems.

progress.text: The ellipsoid method and early interior-point algorithms establish polynomial-time solvability in the total input bit length. They do not provide a general strongly polynomial operation bound.

Tardos gives an algorithm whose arithmetic count is independent of the right-hand side and objective magnitudes, with remaining dependence on the constraint matrix. Small integer entries in that matrix give important strongly polynomial special cases.

Allamigeon, Gaubert, and Vandame construct LP families forcing exponentially many iterations for the self-concordant-barrier path-following methods covered by their theorem. This restricts a route to solving the problem; it is not an unrestricted LP lower bound.

Dadush, Koh, Natura, Olver, and Végh solve minimum-cost generalized flow and LPs with at most two nonzeros per row or column in strongly polynomial time. Their analysis also controls intermediate bit lengths.

Dadush, Ma, Natura, and Végh improve interior-point bounds in terms of straight-line complexity and give strongly polynomial trust-region subroutines. Straight-line complexity can itself be large, so these are not dimension-only bounds for arbitrary LPs.

Version 10 of Awoniyi’s preprint claims at most 2(m+n) complementary-pivot iterations for general LP. This review has not validated the termination/correctness argument and complete bit-complexity guarantee, and found no independent primary confirmation. The claim is not promoted to an established resolution.

context_blocks.text: Linear programming is already solvable in polynomial time when input length includes the bits used to write its coefficients. The unresolved issue is whether the number of arithmetic decisions can depend only on the number of constraints and variables. Very large capacities, costs, or denominators may require long arithmetic operands, but the question asks whether they must also force more arithmetic steps.

Both requirements in the definition are essential. Bounding the number of steps while allowing intermediate integers with exponentially many bits could hide enormous computation inside single arithmetic operations. Bounding only total bit time gives ordinary polynomial-time linear programming, which is already known. The strongly polynomial target combines a dimension-only operation count with controlled numerical representation.

Combinatorial optimization supplies positive examples. Tardos’s method removes dependence on the magnitudes of the right-hand side and objective, and yields strongly polynomial bounds for suitable small-coefficient constraint matrices. More recently, a strongly polynomial algorithm was obtained when each row, or each column, has at most two nonzero entries. These cases show that large numerical data alone need not force many arithmetic steps.

For unrestricted matrices, an algorithm may need a different way to navigate the feasible region. Long central paths can defeat broad classes of path-following methods, even though other approaches remain possible. A separate status issue is a 2025 preprint, revised in July 2026, claiming a general solution. Its claim is recorded below, but this review has not established its correctness or found independent validation.

cards.title: Is exact semidefinite feasibility in polynomial time?
cards.formal: Is the following language in P in the ordinary Turing model: all lists of symmetric rational matrices A_0,A_1,…,A_m∈Q^{n×n} for which there exists a real vector x∈R^m satisfying A_0+sum_{i=1}^m x_i A_i⪰0? Both m and n are unbounded parts of the input, and the algorithm must decide exact nonemptiness in time polynomial in the total binary encoding length.
cards.definitions: Every matrix entry is an explicitly supplied rational number, with signed binary numerator and positive binary denominator; all matrices have the same size n≥1. A symmetric matrix M is positive semidefinite, written M⪰0, when zᵀMz≥0 for every real vector z, equivalently when all eigenvalues are nonnegative. The unknown x ranges over all real vectors, not just rational vectors. Singular feasible matrices count as YES. There is no strict-feasibility, boundedness, conditioning, rank, or distance-to-infeasibility promise, and no radius or accuracy parameter is supplied. The output is one bit specifying whether any feasible x exists; an explicit feasible point is not required. An affine subspace given by rational linear equations can be parametrized by rational Gaussian elimination, so this is also the rational-affine-subspace intersection formulation. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: A basic boundary between numerical convex optimization and exact efficient computation. Resolving it would clarify what semidefinite programming can guarantee without hidden regularity or witness-size assumptions, with consequences for optimization relaxations, algebraic certificates and verification.

importance.reason: A foundational complexity gap in a widely used convex optimization model; exact decision remains open despite powerful approximation algorithms, exact duality and symbolic decidability.

progress.text: Ramana constructs an exact dual without regularity assumptions and proves simultaneous NP/coNP membership in the Turing model, without proving membership in either class.

Henrion, Naldi and Safey El Din develop symbolic homotopy for degenerate feasible sets. Generic auxiliary choices and objectives remain in their algorithmic analysis; fixed-parameter arithmetic bounds are not a general polynomial bit bound.
Pataki and Touzov publish a structural analysis of exponentially large feasible solutions and partial approaches to representing them compactly.
Pataki’s preprint gives a combinatorial treatment of Ramana’s exact dual and its feasible set, preserving the unresolved Turing-model complexity distinction.

Slot, Steurer and Wiedmer prove polynomial bit-length bounds for approximate optima of convex polynomial minimization over polyhedra. The result does not cover exact feasibility of arbitrary linear matrix inequalities.

cards.status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. The primary literature retains general exact SDP feasibility as an open polynomial-time problem. Ramana’s dual does not establish NP∩coNP membership in the Turing model, and recent convex-polynomial optimization results address a different constraint family. This card permits real witnesses, singular feasible points, weak infeasibility and unbounded feasible regions.

context_blocks.text: Semidefinite constraints replace scalar nonnegativity by nonnegativity of a quadratic form in every direction. They include linear inequalities as the diagonal-matrix special case and support powerful relaxations in combinatorial optimization. Approximation algorithms are well developed, but their guarantees require attention to input geometry and numerical precision. De Klerk and Vallentin establish polynomial bit complexity for a short-step interior-point method under appropriate assumptions; their theorem is about controlled approximation, not arbitrary exact feasibility.

The unrestricted problem is decidable. Introduce a real n×n matrix Y and impose A_0+sum_i x_i A_i=YYᵀ. These are finitely many polynomial equations of degree at most two, and a real symmetric matrix is positive semidefinite exactly when such a factor exists. General real-algebraic decision procedures therefore apply. Henrion, Naldi and Safey El Din develop more specialized symbolic algorithms, including treatment of degenerate feasible sets. None of this supplies polynomial time when both input dimensions vary.

Exact feasibility can differ even from arbitrarily close approximation. The matrix M(t) with rows (0,1) and (1,t) has determinant −1, so it is never positive semidefinite. Yet as t tends to positive infinity, its negative eigenvalue (t−√(t²+4))/2 tends to zero. Thus these infeasible matrices approach the positive semidefinite cone arbitrarily closely. A numerical tolerance alone cannot distinguish this situation from a singular feasible matrix.

Rational input also need not admit a rational witness. Consider a block diagonal matrix with blocks [[x,2],[2,2x]] and [[2,x],[x,1]]. The first block is positive semidefinite exactly when x≥√2, and the second when |x|≤√2. The whole matrix is therefore feasible exactly at x=√2. All coefficient matrices are rational, but searching only rational substitutions would miss the solution. This example explains why the domain of the unknowns is part of the formal question.

Even rational feasible points can be enormous. Conditions x_1≥2 and [[x_{i+1},x_i],[x_i,1]]⪰0 force x_{i+1}≥x_i², hence x_k≥2^{2^{k−1}}. A block diagonal LMI encodes the chain compactly, while writing its final coordinate in ordinary binary needs exponentially many digits in k. Pataki and Touzov analyze how such growth arises beyond isolated examples, including connections to singularity degree. Large explicit witnesses obstruct a naive search algorithm; they do not prove that deciding existence is hard.

Ramana’s exact dual provides an alternative feasibility system of polynomial description size without regularity assumptions. In the Turing model, it implies that semidefinite feasibility belongs to NP if and only if it belongs to coNP. It does not establish either membership individually. The corresponding NP∩coNP theorem over exact real-number machines belongs to a different computational model. This distinction prevents a common overstatement of what SDP duality proves about bit complexity.
Pataki’s October 2025 work gives a new derivation and a fuller description of the feasible set of Ramana’s dual using facial reduction.

A separate STOC 2026 result by Slot, Steurer and Wiedmer obtains small approximate solutions for minimizing convex polynomials over polyhedra. That result concerns polynomial objectives with linear constraints; the authors explicitly contrast it with the large-solution obstacle for semidefinite programs. It does not settle general exact semidefinite feasibility.

cards.title: Does the packing property imply the max-flow min-cut property?
cards.formal: Does every finite clutter with the packing property have the max-flow min-cut property? Equivalently, if every deletion/contraction minor satisfies unweighted integral packing–covering equality, must weighted integral packing–covering equality hold for every nonnegative integer weight vector?
cards.definitions: A clutter C on a finite ground set E is a family of subsets of E, no one properly containing another. In the original instance all members are nonempty; the empty family is allowed. A cover T⊆E meets every member, and τ(C) is the smallest cover size. A packing is a family of pairwise disjoint members, with maximum size ν(C). Deleting e removes e from the ground set and discards all members containing e. Contracting e removes it from the ground set and from every member, and retains only inclusion-minimal resulting members. A minor results from any sequence of these operations. The packing property means τ(C′)=ν(C′) for every minor C′. For the empty family both values are zero; for a minor containing the empty set both are defined as +∞, with the empty member permitted arbitrarily many times in a packing. For w∈ℤ_{≥0}^E, let τ_w(C)=min{Σ_{e∈T}w_e:T covers C}. Let ν_w(C) be the maximum of Σ_{F∈C}y_F over nonnegative integers y_F satisfying Σ_{F∋e}y_F≤w_e for every e∈E. Thus a weighted packing may use a member repeatedly, subject to capacities w. The max-flow min-cut property is τ_w(C)=ν_w(C) for every such w. The original nonempty-member assumption makes these weighted optima finite.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that the packing property implies τ_w=ν_w for every finite clutter and every nonnegative integer weight vector, or give a finite clutter and weight vector with the packing property and τ_w>ν_w. A counterexample must verify equality for all minors, not merely for the original unweighted clutter. Finite searches, proofs for a proper subclass, or fractional optimality alone do not resolve the universal statement.

context_blocks.text: Packing and covering often give two descriptions of the same combinatorial optimum. In a clutter, the unweighted equality can fail. Requiring equality after every deletion and contraction removes many such obstructions. The Conforti–Cornuéjols conjecture asks whether this local robustness already guarantees equality for every integer capacity vector.

For a concrete example, take E as the vertices of a bipartite graph and the clutter members as its edges. Covers are vertex covers and packings are matchings. This illustrates the familiar kind of min–max equality that the general conjecture seeks to characterize, without restricting its input to graph edge families.

If A is the member-by-element incidence matrix, the associated linear programs are min wᵀx subject to Ax≥1 and x≥0, and max 1ᵀy subject to Aᵀy≤w and y≥0. Equality of the two integer optima forces their values to agree with the fractional optimum by weak and strong duality. This is the standard MFMC integrality requirement.

Schrijver’s Survey Question 68 calls the target the assertion that every packing hypergraph is Mengerian. The terminology differs, but its packing property includes all minors and its conclusion includes arbitrary nonnegative integer weights. Checking only the all-ones weight on the original instance would yield a much weaker, insufficient hypothesis.

Abdi and Schwarcz’s July 2026 manuscript calls the statement the replication conjecture and explicitly retains it as open. It reports verification for clutters on at most ten elements and for a specified bounded-degree family of cuboids. These are finite or restricted confirmations, not a proof for arbitrary ground-set size.

The same work gives a finite set of weight vectors sufficient to test the MFMC property of a fixed clutter, with an improved bound on their entries. This makes checking individual instances more effective. The number and size of possible clutters still grow without bound, so instance-wise testability does not prove the universal implication.

importance.reason: A central conjecture connecting minor obstructions, integral linear programming and packing–covering duality. Schrijver treats it as a major survey question, and a July 2026 primary paper develops both theoretical and computational methods around it.

cards.title: Nearly linear-time solution of general sparse linear systems
cards.formal: For every fixed integer c≥1, does there exist a uniform randomized classical algorithm A_c with the following guarantee? Given n≥2, a nonsingular rational n×n matrix A with m nonzero entries, a nonzero rational vector b, and an integer 1≤p≤c·ceil(log_2 n), output a rational vector x̂ such that ||Ax̂−b||_2≤2^(−p)||b||_2 with probability at least 2/3. Each numerator and positive denominator of A and b has at most c·ceil(log_2 n) binary digits, and the spectral condition number κ_2(A) is promised at most n^c. The worst-case running time must be O_c(m log^(d_c)n) for some constant d_c independent of the input.
cards.definitions: The input lists the row index, column index and rational value of each nonzero coefficient, without duplicate positions, together with the n entries of b; hence n≤m≤n². The Euclidean norm is ||v||_2=(Σ_i v_i²)^(1/2), and κ_2(A)=σ_max(A)/σ_min(A), the ratio of its largest and smallest singular values. Nonsingularity makes the denominator positive. A may be nonsymmetric, indefinite and unrelated to a graph Laplacian. The algorithm need only meet its guarantee on promised inputs; it is not asked to certify the condition-number promise. Computation uses a word RAM with Θ(log n)-bit words, conventional arithmetic, comparison, bit operations and memory access; all operations on longer numbers, preprocessing, random-bit generation and writing the output are charged. No operation on an arbitrary real number has unit cost. Converting word operations to bit operations changes only polylogarithmic factors. Constants and the fixed program may depend on c, but neither nonuniform advice depending on n nor a supplied inverse or preconditioner is allowed. Here ε=2^(−p); this is the polynomial-condition, inverse-polynomial-accuracy regime of the near-input-size target. The output is the full list of n rational coordinates, each as a signed binary numerator and positive binary denominator; every output bit is charged. The word instructions are random-access reads/writes, comparisons, conditional branches, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo 2^w, integer quotient/remainder with nonzero divisor, bitwise Boolean operations, and shifts of a w-bit word; shifts by at least w yield zero. The constant in word length w=Θ(log n) (or Θ(log N) when N is the stated input size) is fixed with the algorithm. Address arithmetic has the same cost, larger integers occupy multiple words, and no instruction performs arbitrary-precision arithmetic in one step. When randomization is allowed, a fresh independent uniform w-bit word costs one operation.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: This tests whether sparsity and moderate conditioning suffice for solving linear equations at essentially the cost of reading them. A resolution would clarify the limits of graph-based solvers, preconditioning and numerical subroutines used throughout algorithms and optimization.

importance.reason: A fundamental input-size complexity question for one of the most widely used computational primitives, with meaningful positive results for structured classes and general reductions from apparently special systems.

The Simons workshop report is revised to reflect status through 20 August, retaining questions about extending scalable solvers and understanding finite-precision iterative methods. It does not give a universal nearly linear algorithm.

cards.status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. This is an editorial, fully specified near-linear target in the polynomial-conditioning and precision regime, not a named positive conjecture. The faster-than-matrix-multiplication problem has already been solved. The August 2026 report discusses broader scalable solvers but does not claim this universal guarantee; the simplicial-Laplacian reduction is not a general running-time lower bound.

context_blocks.text: Solving Ax=b is a basic operation inside scientific simulation, optimization and data analysis. A sparse input can be read and multiplied by a vector without scanning all n² matrix positions. The question is whether solving one system can always be comparably inexpensive, up to powers of logarithms. Peng and Vempala frame the general complexity problem around exploiting sparsity while also controlling numerical precision, rather than treating arithmetic on exact real numbers as free.

The target fixes a residual norm because different meanings of approximate solution can conceal different costs. If x*=A^(-1)b, the elementary inequality ||x̂−x*||_2/||x*||_2≤κ_2(A)·||Ax̂−b||_2/||b||_2 relates residual error to forward error. Thus a tiny residual need not mean an equally tiny solution error. For instance, A=diag(1,δ), b=(1,δ) and x̂=(1,0) have residual δ while the second solution coordinate is wrong by one. The condition promise and requested accuracy make this dependence explicit.

Nearly linear solvers already exist for major structured families. Spielman and Teng establish such algorithms for symmetric diagonally dominant systems using preconditioning and graph structure. Their guarantee is naturally expressed in the matrix energy norm. For positive-definite systems, norm comparisons relate this guarantee to residual accuracy, with conditioning affecting the required tolerance. An arbitrary sparse matrix lacks the diagonal-dominance structure that supports this machinery.

Peng and Vempala’s SODA 2021 result breaks the matrix-multiplication barrier for sufficiently sparse, polynomially conditioned systems. They implement a randomized block Krylov approach using structured factorizations and a numerical-stability analysis. This is why merely asking for a sparse solver faster than matrix multiplication would be an obsolete open question. The stronger near-input-size target remains far beyond that theorem.

Nie improves the required anti-concentration bounds for random Krylov matrices. His STOC 2022 result yields a bound of Õ(m^((ω−2)/(ω−1))n²) in the polynomial-conditioning and precision regime. For m=Õ(n), this becomes Õ(n^((3ω−4)/(ω−1))). The paper’s numerical exponent 2.2716 uses the matrix-multiplication bound available at that time; it is not a claim about today’s best numerical value of ω. Either expression remains far above linear for very sparse inputs.

The distinction between a sparse matrix and a structurally easy sparse matrix is sharpened by Ding, Kyng, Probst Gutenberg and Zhang. They reduce general linear equations with polynomially bounded integer coefficients and conditioning to Laplacians of two-dimensional simplicial complexes while preserving sparsity up to logarithmic factors. Consequently, extending graph-Laplacian techniques to those higher-dimensional Laplacians would already have general consequences. This is a completeness reduction, not an unconditional proof that a near-linear solver cannot exist.

The Simons workshop report, revised in August 2026, calls for broader classes of scalably solvable systems and studies the finite-precision behavior of iterative methods. Its benchmark questions are more focused than a universal worst-case solver, and its discussion of preconditioning makes clear that constructing a useful preconditioner is itself part of the computational task. The present card is an explicit editorial formulation of the general complexity target; it is not attributed to a numbered conjecture in that report.

The output requirement also matters. An explicit n-vector is compatible with nearly linear time because a nonsingular n×n input has at least n nonzeros. Returning only access to a vector, a few observables, or a quantum state encoding its normalized coordinates changes the task. Conversely, demanding an exact rational solution could introduce much larger output encodings; the specified numerical approximation avoids building that extra requirement into the question.

cards.formal: Do there exist constants C,K>0, an integer k≥1 and a deterministic real-number algorithm A in the model below such that, for every integer N≥2, A(N) outputs N distinct points x₁,…,x_N on S² in at most KN^k operations and E_N(x₁,…,x_N)≤E_N*+C ln N?

cards.definitions: S²={x∈ℝ³: x₁²+x₂²+x₃²=1}. The energy is E_N(x₁,…,x_N)=Σ_{i≠j}−ln‖x_i−x_j‖₂, counting ordered pairs; collisions have energy +∞. E_N* is the infimum over all N-tuples on S². ln is the natural logarithm and ‖·‖₂ is Euclidean distance. The algorithm is one finite real-arithmetic program with a fixed finite list of real constants, independent of N. It has exact real registers and a finite-control tape machine with register copying, addition, subtraction, multiplication, division by a nonzero register, and branching on the sign of a register. Tape movements and each scalar arithmetic, comparison or copy operation have unit cost. Input is the integer N as an exact real value; output is a list of 3N real coordinates. Any finite tape/register storage used by the program is charged through its operations. There is no primitive logarithm, square root, floor, random sample or minimization oracle. Polynomial time is in N, not in log N. The inequality is a mathematical condition on the output; the algorithm need not evaluate the energy. This specifies the real-number computation convention in Smale’s problem; coordinates need not be rational and no bit-cost bound is asserted.
cards.answer_criterion: A positive answer supplies one permitted real-arithmetic program and constants C,K,k, fixed independently of N, with the stated running time and total-energy guarantee for every integer N≥2. A negative answer proves that no such program and constants exist. Failure of one construction, a lower bound for a restricted method, or energy estimates for finitely many cardinalities do not establish the negation.

references.locator: Problem 7; real-number computation model and logarithmic excess energy.

context_blocks.text: Imagine placing mutually repelling particles on a sphere. For this problem, a pair contributes minus the logarithm of its straight-line distance through three-dimensional space. Bringing two points together sends their contribution to positive infinity. Spreading points lowers the energy, but the question asks for a guarantee against the best configuration of the entire collection, rather than against a locally stable arrangement. Exact minimizers are called elliptic Fekete configurations.

For two points the answer is concrete: opposite poles have distance 2, the largest possible distance on the unit sphere, and ordered-pair energy −2 ln 2. For general N an optimum still exists: the sphere is compact, collisions have infinite energy, and some distinct configuration has finite energy. Existence therefore is not the open part. The unresolved requirement is one fixed algorithm with a polynomial operation bound for every N.

The tolerance C ln N is an additive error in the total energy. It is small compared with its known expansion E_N*=(1/2−ln 2)N²−(N/2)ln N+aN+o(N), where a is a universal constant. Matching only the leading N² term, or even allowing a linear error, leaves far more uncertainty than the target permits. Uniform-looking points and good numerical values for finitely many N do not establish this error bound.

Smale’s original statement counts each unordered pair once. This card counts each pair twice, as in much subsequent literature. Both the optimum and excess energy are doubled, so the existence of a universal logarithmic-error constant is unchanged. The real-arithmetic model also comes from Smale’s formulation: a step manipulates an exact real value. A polynomial number of such steps does not assert polynomial bit complexity, and the output inequality does not give the program a free logarithm or minimization instruction.

The generalized Diamond ensemble supplies configurations for every N with a precisely analyzed expected energy: the two leading terms above plus a specified linear term and an O(√N ln N) remainder. These constructions quantify how well a structured distribution spreads points. That estimate is not a deterministic C ln N excess guarantee relative to the unknown optimum.

Beltrán and Hardy obtain the required logarithmic excess for a low-temperature Coulomb-gas distribution: at inverse temperature N, the mean excess is at most 9 ln N, and excess at most 10 ln N holds with probability at least 1−exp(−N ln N). The theorem analyzes the distribution, while polynomial-time sampling from it remains an additional computational issue. A probabilistic existence statement also differs from the deterministic algorithm asked for here.

Michelen and Yakir prove a central limit theorem for the energy of zeros of a rotationally invariant random polynomial, with fluctuations on the √N scale. This measures variation around that ensemble’s mean, not error from the global minimum.

Recent exact algebraic work by Armentano and coauthors classifies critical configurations with at most six points, and treats seven points under an antipodal-pair restriction. Such finite classifications do not supply a uniform algorithm for arbitrary N.

The original motivation connects low-energy spherical points, through stereographic projection, to well-conditioned polynomials and the complexity of finding polynomial roots. The energy question has its own stronger output guarantee; progress on polynomial conditioning or on a different Smale problem does not automatically resolve it. It also asks a basic algorithmic question in discrete potential theory: how cheaply can globally near-equilibrium configurations be constructed?

The theorem analyzes the distribution, while polynomial-time sampling from it remains an additional computational issue. A probabilistic existence statement also differs from the deterministic algorithm asked for here.

Michelen and Yakir prove a central limit theorem for the energy of zeros of a rotationally invariant random polynomial, with fluctuations on the √N scale. This measures variation around that ensemble’s mean, not error from the global minimum.

Recent exact algebraic work by Armentano and coauthors classifies critical configurations with at most six points, and treats seven points under an antipodal-pair restriction. Such finite classifications do not supply a uniform algorithm for arbitrary N.

The original motivation connects low-energy spherical points, through stereographic projection, to well-conditioned polynomials and the complexity of finding polynomial roots. The energy question has its own stronger output guarantee; progress on polynomial conditioning or on a different Smale problem does not automatically resolve it. It also asks a basic algorithmic question in discrete potential theory: how cheaply can globally near-equilibrium configurations be constructed?

cards.title: Does every isotropic log-concave measure have a dimension-free Poincaré constant?
cards.formal: Does there exist a universal constant C<∞ such that, for every dimension n≥1, every isotropic log-concave probability measure μ on ℝⁿ, and every locally Lipschitz f:ℝⁿ→ℝ with finite second moment and finite gradient energy, $\operatorname{Var}_\mu(f)\le C\int\|\nabla f(x)\|_2^2\,d\mu(x)$? This is the Poincaré formulation of the Kannan–Lovász–Simonovits conjecture.
cards.definitions: The measure has a Lebesgue density ρ=e^{−V}, where V:ℝⁿ→ℝ∪{+∞} is convex and ∫ρ=1; allowing V=+∞ includes uniform distributions on full-dimensional convex bodies. Isotropy means ∫x dμ(x)=0 and ∫xxᵀ dμ(x)=Iₙ. Variance is Varμ(f)=∫(f−∫f dμ)²dμ, and ∇f is the almost-everywhere Euclidean gradient. Let C_P(μ) be the infimum of constants that make the displayed inequality hold for all the stated f. The requested bound is supₙ supμ C_P(μ)<∞, with μ ranging over isotropic log-concave measures in ℝⁿ. There is no symmetry, product structure, smoothness, or positive lower curvature bound on V. The universal constant may depend on none of n, μ, or f. In the isoperimetric convention used by the recent papers, ψμ is the reciprocal Cheeger expansion constant; ψμ² is comparable to C_P(μ) up to universal factors. Thus a bound on ψμ must be squared when expressed as a bound on the Poincaré constant used here.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: KLS links the geometry of high-dimensional convex sets to spectral gaps, concentration, and the efficiency of sampling. It asks whether covariance normalization alone removes every dimension-dependent bottleneck for log-concave measures, making it a central structural question behind continuous randomized algorithms.

importance.reason: A foundational high-dimensional geometry conjecture with substantial consequences for sampling, integration, optimization, and concentration inequalities.

progress.text: Kannan, Lovász, and Simonovits formulate the isoperimetric conjecture in connection with localization and random-walk sampling in convex bodies.

Klartag and Lehec settle the thin-shell conjecture. The 23 February 2026 revision controls E(‖X‖₂−√n)² uniformly, a particular radial concentration target rather than the full Poincaré inequality.

Letwin’s preprint reports Var(XᵀMX)≤2E‖∇(XᵀMX)‖₂² for every symmetric M and isotropic log-concave X, and derives ψₙ=O((log n)^{1/4}). In this card’s normalization the resulting general-function bound is C_P=O(√log n), not O((log n)^{1/4}).

context_blocks.text: The inequality asks whether a function can vary substantially across a log-concave distribution while changing only slowly in the regions where that distribution places mass. Isotropy fixes the scale: each unit-direction linear function already has variance one and gradient energy one. The conjecture says that nonlinear functions cannot create an arbitrarily larger ratio as dimension grows.

The geometric version rules out a hidden bottleneck separating two substantial portions of the measure. For a log-concave density, the conjecture says that the best arbitrary separating set has boundary expansion comparable to an appropriate halfspace cut. Uniform distributions on convex bodies are included, so the question is not confined to smooth, strongly convex potentials where curvature can directly control a spectral gap.

The original algorithmic motivation was sampling by random walks. Poor expansion can trap a local walk in one part of a body for a long time; good expansion bounds its mixing. Sampling then supports volume estimation, integration, and convex optimization. A KLS theorem would improve the geometric ingredient in these analyses, though total algorithmic complexity would still account for access to the body, initialization, and the chosen walk.

Thin-shell concentration concerns the special observable ‖X‖₂. Klartag and Lehec’s 2025 result, revised in February 2026, bounds E(‖X‖₂−√n)² by a universal constant. This settles thin-shell concentration and also supports the resolved slicing question, but does not by itself control every test function in the Poincaré inequality. These neighboring geometric conjectures must therefore be tracked separately.

The remaining dimension dependence is small but substantive. Klartag’s 2023 theorem gives C_P(μ)=O(log n). Letwin’s July 2026 preprint reports a dimension-free inequality for quadratic forms and derives ψμ=O((log n)^{1/4}), hence C_P(μ)=O(√log n). The latter is a reported preprint improvement, and even that estimate still leaves a growing factor rather than the universal constant required here.

cards.title: Gupta–Newman–Rabinovich–Sinclair conjecture
cards.formal: For every fixed finite simple graph H, is there a finite constant C_H≥1 such that, for every finite connected simple undirected H-minor-free graph G with strictly positive real edge lengths, its shortest-path metric d_G admits a map f:V(G)→ℝᵐ into some finite-dimensional ℓ₁ space satisfying d_G(u,v)≤‖f(u)−f(v)‖₁≤C_H d_G(u,v) for all vertices u,v?
cards.definitions: H-minor-free means that deleting vertices and edges and contracting edges of G cannot produce a graph isomorphic to H, after removing loops and duplicate edges. The length of a path is the sum of its edge lengths, and d_G(u,v) is the minimum path length. In ℝᵐ, ‖x−y‖₁=Σⱼ₌₁ᵐ |xⱼ−yⱼ|. The displayed inequalities normalize the embedding to be noncontracting; permitting a common scaling factor gives the same distortion notion. The constant C_H may depend on the excluded graph H, but must be independent of |V(G)|, the edge lengths and their ratio. The target dimension m and the map f may depend on the entire weighted graph and have no computational or dimension bound. This is an existence question for all vertex pairs simultaneously. It concerns undirected shortest-path distances themselves, without a snowflake transformation, average-pair guarantee or restriction to selected terminals.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: Determine whether excluded graph minors exactly prevent unbounded ℓ₁ distortion and multicommodity flow–cut gaps in proper minor-closed graph families.

Restricted-family and face-cover results, including February 2026 exact values for K₂,ₙ, do not settle arbitrary fixed-minor-free metrics. context_blocks.text: The conjecture asks whether excluding a fixed graph minor removes every large-scale obstruction to representing graph distances as sums of coordinate differences. The graph can have arbitrarily many vertices and very unequal edge lengths. Its topology supplies the restriction, while the conclusion concerns the metric generated by all those lengths. Gupta, Newman, Rabinovich and Sinclair formulate this connection in their work on cuts, trees and ℓ₁ embeddings.

The target ℓ₁ space is useful because its finite metrics are nonnegative combinations of cut metrics. A cut metric assigns distance one to pairs separated by a chosen vertex subset and zero to other pairs. Coordinates can be decomposed by thresholding their values, producing precisely such cuts. Thus an ℓ₁ embedding replaces a complicated distance function by weighted separation tests that are closely connected to graph partitioning.

Trees give a concrete exact example. Root a weighted tree and assign one coordinate to each edge. For that coordinate, give a vertex the edge’s length if it lies below the edge and zero otherwise. Two vertices differ in exactly the coordinates corresponding to their unique connecting path. Their ℓ₁ distance therefore equals their original tree distance. Cycles allow competing shortest paths, which makes a common coordinate representation much harder.

The equivalent flow formulation compares two bounds on simultaneous routing. A concurrent flow routes the same fraction of every specified pair’s demand through a capacitated graph, splitting traffic among paths when useful. Every cut bounds that fraction by its available capacity divided by the demand it separates. GNRS predicts that, on any fixed-minor-free family, the best cut bound exceeds the achievable concurrent-flow value by at most a family-dependent constant, for arbitrary nonnegative demands.

Arbitrary demands are essential. Restricting to uniform demand between all vertex pairs gives an easier problem with stronger known results. Likewise, the capacity graph can be minor-free while demand pairs connect vertices in any pattern. Requiring the demands themselves to form a planar graph would change the target. The geometric formulation avoids these auxiliary conventions by requiring distance preservation for every vertex pair.

The planar case remains a central unresolved test. Rao’s general guarantee is O(√log n) distortion for n-vertex planar metrics, and Chekuri’s May 2026 lecture notes still list a constant bound as open. No growing lower bound for planar metrics is known in that account. Both a constant upper bound and a superconstant counterexample would therefore represent a substantial change in understanding.

Several restricted families do satisfy constant distortion bounds. The original work handles series-parallel graphs. Lee and Sidiropoulos prove a stronger random-tree embedding result for graphs of any fixed pathwidth k, with distortion depending only on k. Their theorem establishes GNRS for minor-closed families that exclude a tree. Fixed pathwidth is a substantial additional restriction and does not include all graphs of fixed treewidth.

This last distinction exposes a common pitfall in reading algorithmic progress. Chlamtac, Krauthgamer and Raghavendra obtain constant-factor sparsest-cut approximation on every fixed-treewidth class using the Sherali–Adams hierarchy. They explicitly explain that their stronger relaxation does not establish a constant gap for the ordinary concurrent-flow LP. Thus the inherited paper is important context and an algorithmic success, but it is not a proof of the bounded-treewidth case of GNRS.

Filtser improves a terminal-sensitive planar bound: when the terminals can be covered by γ faces of a planar drawing, their metric embeds with distortion O(√log(γ+1)). The added one simply handles the single-face case in asymptotic notation. This is constant for fixed γ and recovers the familiar n-dependent bound when all vertices require many faces. The 2024 journal-online publication refines which geometric parameter creates the loss.

There is also recent exact progress inside small planar families. Mori’s February 2026 preprint calculates the worst-over-edge-lengths distortion of K₂,ₙ as (3k−2)/(2k−1), where k=⌈n/2⌉. The values approach 3/2. This demonstrates a nontrivial bounded loss in an infinite family, rather than a counterexample with distortion growing without bound. Such examples help test the sharpness and limitations of proposed embedding mechanisms.

A solution would connect a qualitative structural restriction—excluding one fixed minor—to a uniform quantitative statement about all distances and all concurrent-routing instances. It would explain whether the logarithmic losses in current general embedding arguments are unavoidable on these graph families. The question remains meaningful independently of how efficiently the embedding can be constructed.

cards.title: Unknot recognition in polynomial time
cards.formal: Is there a deterministic Turing algorithm and a constant c such that, on every explicit combinatorial knot diagram D of encoding length N, the algorithm decides in O((N+1)^c) bit operations whether the represented knot in the 3-sphere is ambient isotopic to the unknot?
cards.definitions: A knot is a tame embedding of one circle into S³; the unknot is the isotopy class of a round circle. Ambient isotopy means a continuous family of homeomorphisms of S³ starting at the identity and carrying one embedded circle to the other at its endpoint. A diagram is a generic projection with transverse double crossings and specified over/under information. Encode it by an explicitly listed connected 4-regular planar multigraph, including loops when needed, its cyclic orders of half-edges at vertices, a distinguished outer face and the overpassing pair of opposite half-edges at each crossing. Tracing the opposite pairs must give one component. A separate constant-size encoding represents the crossing-free circle. The embedding is required to be a valid sphere embedding; malformed encodings may be rejected by polynomial-time combinatorial checks. If the diagram has n crossings, a standard such encoding has O(n log(n+1)) bits. The complexity parameter is the supplied encoding length N, not the minimum crossing number among equivalent diagrams. The input is explicit rather than a compressed description of an exponentially larger diagram. No disk, simplification sequence, knot invariant, auxiliary advice or promise of triviality is supplied. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: Determine whether triviality of an explicitly given knot can be decided efficiently, a foundational test of the gap between topological certificates and algorithms.

importance.reason: A central algorithmic topology problem in NP∩coNP; a fresh claimed polynomial-time solution makes precise formulation and validation especially valuable.

cards.status_note: Musick’s 6 September 2026 preprint claims a polynomial-time solution. Its correctness has not been independently established in this review, so the card is not labelled either a settled theorem or an unqualified open problem. Established certificates and earlier algorithmic results are distinguished from this new claim. Checked through 11 September 2026.

context_blocks.text: Status requires special care: Chad Musick’s preprint of 6 September 2026 claims a positive answer in Corollary 1. Its route is a polynomial-time construction of a locally minimal bridge presentation using compressed descriptions, followed by an existing characterization of bridge presentations of the unknot. I checked the claim and its main proof dependencies, but have not independently verified the local-minimality argument or compressed-update complexity. The card is therefore marked uncertain pending validation of this fresh claimed resolution.

The underlying task is deceptively simple: determine whether a closed loop can be untangled without cutting it or passing one strand through another. A diagram can contain many crossings that are artifacts of its projection. Looking complicated does not prove knottedness, while repeatedly removing visible twists can get stuck on a diagram that still represents the unknot. The input can be deliberately chosen to frustrate familiar simplification strategies.

The chosen representation makes the computational question independent of numerical geometry. Coordinates, thickness, physical forces and drawing quality do not enter the running time. Cyclic orders record the planar embedding, and the crossing data tell us which strand passes over the other. The task concerns the topology represented by those finite combinatorial data, not the visual complexity of a particular rendering.

Hass, Lagarias and Pippenger prove that unknot recognition belongs to NP using normal-surface techniques. Informally, an unknot bounds an embedded disk, and a suitable disk can be encoded compactly through its intersections with tetrahedra in a triangulation. Large counts are stored in binary. The existence of a polynomial-size verifiable certificate gives an upper bound on nondeterministic complexity, while finding such a certificate may still require substantial search.

Lackenby proves that knottedness also belongs to NP, so unknot recognition lies in coNP as well. This is an unconditional theorem, unlike earlier approaches that required the generalized Riemann hypothesis. It places the problem in NP∩coNP and makes ordinary NP-completeness unlikely: an NP-hard language in coNP would imply NP=coNP. Membership in both classes does not itself give a polynomial-time decision algorithm.

cards.title: Polynomial Hirsch conjecture for edge-path diameter
cards.formal: Do universal constants C>0 and k≥1 exist such that every nonempty pointed d-dimensional convex polyhedron with n facets has vertex-edge graph diameter at most C(n+d)^k?
cards.definitions: A polyhedron is an intersection of finitely many closed affine halfspaces over the real numbers. Work in its affine hull, identified with R^d, where d≥1, and require it to be pointed, meaning that it contains no affine line; this ensures that its vertices are present. Both bounded polyhedra, called polytopes, and unbounded pointed polyhedra are included. The number n counts distinct facets in an irredundant description, rather than repeated input inequalities. The graph G(P) has one vertex per geometric vertex of P and an undirected edge between u and v precisely when their segment is a bounded one-dimensional face of P. An unbounded ray is not an extra graph vertex or an edge to infinity. Graph distance counts edges, each at unit cost; diameter is the maximum distance between vertices and is zero for a one-vertex polyhedron. The constants C,k must be independent of dimension, facet count, coordinates, coefficient bit length and the choice of polyhedron. Real coordinates are allowed, and no simplicity or nondegeneracy assumption is made. Paths need not improve any objective function, and no algorithm for finding them is required.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: Determine whether all polyhedral feasible regions have uniformly short edge routes, a central structural question underlying linear programming.

importance.reason: The surviving fundamental diameter question after the original Hirsch bound failed; it separates geometric existence of short routes from algorithmic navigation and the newly resolved circuit analogue.

cards.status_note: No polynomial upper bound or superpolynomial counterexample for the stated worst-case edge-diameter problem was found through 11 September 2026. Natura’s 2026 result resolves the circuit analogue and explicitly leaves the combinatorial problem open. The card includes bounded and pointed unbounded polyhedra, counts facets, and imposes neither monotonicity nor an efficient path-finding requirement.

context_blocks.text: The feasible region of a linear program is a polyhedron. Its vertices are candidate basic feasible solutions, and its edges describe elementary geometric moves between them. The diameter asks for the largest minimum number of such moves between any two vertices. It is therefore a question about the geometry of feasible solutions before one chooses a particular rule for navigating them.

The facet count is the relevant measure of description size here. A polyhedron described by a modest number of inequalities can have exponentially many vertices, so the trivial bound by the number of vertices is far too large. The d-dimensional cube illustrates the distinction: it has 2d facets and 2^d vertices, yet its diameter is only d because one can change differing coordinates one at a time.

Polynomial means a fixed exponent that works in every dimension. An n^d upper bound is polynomial in n when d is held fixed, but does not answer this question. Neither does a bound whose constant grows exponentially with d. The card includes pointed unbounded polyhedra, matching the saved formulation; pointedness removes polyhedra with no vertices, for which a vertex-graph diameter would not express the intended problem.

Hirsch originally proposed the much sharper n−d bound for bounded polytopes. Santos’s counterexample, announced in 2010 and published in 2012, has dimension 43 and 86 facets, with diameter exceeding 43. This refutes that linear expression, but it remains fully compatible with a bound such as Cn² or Cn¹⁰. The distinction between failure of one attractive formula and failure of every polynomial is the reason a major open question survived.

General upper bounds are quasipolynomial. Kalai and Kleitman’s 1992 argument gave n^{2+log₂d}; Todd improved it in 2014 to (n−d)^{log₂d}. For large d, Sukegawa’s later asymptotic refinement has the form (n−d)^{log₂d−log₂log d+O(1)}. The last exponent still grows with dimension. These are substantial structural bounds, but they do not reach one universal constant exponent.

The conjecture concerns shortest available paths, not the paths a chosen simplex pivot rule happens to take. A rule may visit exponentially many vertices even on a polytope whose graph has small diameter. Conversely, proving that short undirected paths exist would not tell a solver which edge to select efficiently, or ensure a short path that improves a specified linear objective at every step. Polynomial diameter is a geometric ingredient, not by itself a strongly polynomial linear-programming algorithm.

Recent complexity results make the distinction sharper. Wulf’s FOCS 2025 paper proves Π₂^p-hardness of computing the diameter of bipartite perfect-matching polytopes, and the corresponding decision problem is complete for that class. Such hardness is compatible with a polynomial upper bound on the value of the diameter. A small optimum can be difficult to compute exactly, just as short witnesses can be difficult to find.

Natura’s February 2026 paper proves a polynomial bound for a different geometric distance: circuit diameter. For a standard-form polyhedron {x∈R^N:Ax=b,x≥0}, with A having r rows, the stated bound is O(r²log r), and the construction also supplies monotone circuit walks. Circuit directions are support-minimal dependencies of A; a maximal feasible step in such a direction need not stay on an edge of the current polyhedron.

Every edge step is allowed among the circuit moves, but the converse fails. Consequently, a short circuit walk gives no automatic equally short edge walk: its intermediate points may lie inside higher-dimensional faces. The 2026 theorem settles the circuit analogue of the polynomial conjecture, while its introduction explicitly retains the ordinary combinatorial-diameter problem. The distinction is geometric, not a question of hiding logarithmic factors.

Other positive results exploit extra structure, such as totally unimodular constraint matrices or numerical bounds on subdeterminants. Those assumptions control features absent from the unrestricted statement. Random-polytope and smoothed analyses likewise describe particular distributions or perturbations; a worst-case theorem must include every allowed realization. This is why the model specifies arbitrary coefficients and requires constants independent of their encoding.

A positive resolution would reveal a universal short-route property of all polyhedral feasible regions, despite their potentially enormous vertex sets. A negative resolution would produce polyhedra on which every route between some vertices is intrinsically long. Both outcomes would identify a basic geometric limit underlying pivot-based optimization, independently of the performance of any individual implementation.

cards.title: How many k-element subsets can a line separate from a planar point set?
cards.formal: Let K₂(n,k) be the maximum, over sets P of n distinct points in $\mathbb R^2$ with no three collinear, of the number of distinct subsets S⊆P of size k strictly separable from P\S by a line. Determine K₂(n,k) up to universal constant factors, uniformly for all integers n≥2 and 1≤k≤⌊n/2⌋.
cards.definitions: Strict separation means that there are real a,b,c with (a,b)≠(0,0), ax+by<c for every (x,y)∈S, and ax+by>c for every (x,y)∈P\S. The objects counted are subsets S, not their infinitely many possible separating lines. Coordinates have no bounded-precision, grid, or random-distribution promise. The target is worst-case combinatorial complexity, not the running time of an enumeration algorithm. A matching bound means an asymptotic expression F(n,k) and absolute constants 0<c₀≤C₀<∞ such that c₀F(n,k)≤K₂(n,k)≤C₀F(n,k) throughout the stated range, apart from finitely many n which can be absorbed into the constants. Bounds must cover k that grows with n. Complementation supplies the remaining values n/2<k<n; k=0,n each have one subset. This card specializes the original all-dimensions problem to the plane.
cards.answer_criterion: Formulation unfinished. K₂(n,k) and the uniform constant-factor target are defined, but the admissible representation of the answer F(n,k) is not. Allowing arbitrary functions admits F=K₂ itself, while an arbitrarily imposed expression grammar or computational bound would change the question. An answer representation must be selected before this is a closed benchmark specification.
cards.why: A central unresolved counting problem in computational geometry, it controls the complexity of levels and line-separated ranges. Its persistent gap tests the strength of crossing-number methods and geometric constructions, with consequences for output-sensitive and parametric algorithms.

importance.reason: A defining extremal-complexity question for geometric algorithms, already unresolved in the plane and connected to levels, geometric selection, and parametric optimization.

progress.text: Dey proves K₂(n,k)=O(n k^(1/3)) for 1≤k≤n/2 through a crossing-number argument. The balanced specialization gives an O(n^(4/3)) upper bound.
Tóth constructs planar point sets with n exp(Ω(√log k)) k-sets for n≥2k>0, improving the earlier n log k scale. This remains separated from the upper bound by an unbounded factor when k grows.
Nivasch gives a simpler halving-edge construction improving the constant in the square-root-log exponent. The construction does not produce n^(1+ε) halving edges for any fixed positive ε.

Alonso, López, and Rodrigo improve a linear subtractive term in the upper bound on the maximum number of halving lines for even n, and improve some finite-n bounds. The asymptotic upper exponent remains 4/3.
The revised Open Problems Project entry still lists the planar asymptotic gap as unresolved. A search through September 2026 did not locate matching general upper and lower bounds.

context_blocks.text: A line can realize only a small fraction of all choices of k points. The question measures the combinatorial capacity of one linear cut at a fixed output size. For example, when k=1 the separable points are the convex-hull vertices, and their maximum number is n. The difficult regime lets k increase with the input size.

Point-line duality translates changes of a separating line into the structure of levels in a line arrangement. A level tracks positions having a specified number of lines below them. These level bounds recur in geometric selection and in analyses of parametric optimization. Dey’s method also yields bounds for related level structures, convex chains, and parametric spanning-tree problems.

For even n, the balanced case is closely tied to halving edges: segments joining two input points whose supporting line leaves (n−2)/2 of the other points on each side. A halving edge is not itself a separating line, since it passes through input points. The correspondence between k-sets and directed (k−1)-edges gives K₂(n,n/2) equal to twice the maximum number of undirected halving edges.

The known planar upper bound is O(n k^(1/3)), whereas constructions give n exp(Ω(√log k)) subsets. In the balanced regime the latter grows faster than n times any fixed power of log n, yet slower than n^(1+ε) for each fixed ε>0. Thus neither a linear bound nor an ordinary polylogarithmic correction to linear growth can describe the worst case.

Sharper finite-size constructions and improvements to the additive terms of halving-line bounds are useful progress. They do not close the gap in asymptotic growth. Keeping this distinction explicit matters here: an improved upper bound may retain the same 4/3 exponent in the balanced case.

cards.title: Does every VC class admit linear-size sample compression?
cards.formal: Is there a universal constant C such that every nonempty binary concept class H⊆{0,1}^X of finite VC dimension d≥1 admits a labeled sample compression scheme with kernel bound k and side-information bound b satisfying k+b≤Cd, in the model below? The same compressor and reconstructor must work for every finite H-realizable sample, independently of its size.
cards.definitions: The domain X is an arbitrary set, and a concept h∈H is a total function X→{0,1}. A finite set A⊆X is shattered if {h|_A:h∈H}={0,1}^A; d is the largest cardinality of a shattered set. A realizable sample is a finite set S⊆X×{0,1} agreeing with some h∈H. A scheme consists of deterministic maps κ and ρ, which may depend on H, and nonnegative integers k,b. For every realizable S, κ(S)=(T,z), where T⊆S is an unordered labeled subset with |T|≤k and z∈{0,1}^b. The reconstructor receives only T and z and produces a total predictor ρ(T,z):X→{0,1} agreeing with every pair in S. It does not receive S, its size, the omitted points, or their indices. The side string has fixed length b; padding shorter strings changes only constant-factor size conventions. Reconstruction need not lie in H, be stable under deleting unused examples, or have any prescribed computational complexity. No probability distribution, efficiency, or measurability condition is part of this combinatorial existence question. Dimension zero is harmless: a nonempty such class has one labeling and needs no stored examples.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: A central question connecting the combinatorial complexity of prediction with how many observations suffice to represent all training decisions. Its universality across concept classes, and its links to learning, extremal set systems and graph geometry, make the linear-versus-exponential gap fundamental.

context_blocks.text: The stored object is a small selection of examples that lets a fixed decoding rule recover every training label. It need not identify the unknown target function on points never observed. For example, consider indicators of closed intervals on the real line. Retain the leftmost and rightmost positive examples, or the empty set if there are no positives. Decode to the interval between those retained points, or to the all-zero function in the empty case. Realizability ensures that no negative example lies between the extreme positives. Thus an arbitrarily large sample can be represented by at most two examples.

The distinction between examples and bits is essential. A real-valued example may itself require arbitrarily many bits to describe; sample compression charges one unit for retaining it. Conversely, permitting an arbitrary uncharged side message would trivialize the problem, because that message could encode the whole sample. The fixed reconstructor and the explicit bound b prevent this loophole. The question concerns the combinatorial information carried by selected observations, rather than ordinary lossless compression of their numerical representations.

Moran and Yehudayoff proved that every finite-VC binary class has a scheme of size 2^{O(d)}, settling the earlier existence question. Their argument combines learning with an approximate minimax principle. More precisely, their bound also involves the dual VC dimension: this reverses the roles of domain points and concepts, treating each point as its pattern of membership across the concepts. Since the dual dimension can be exponential in d, that result leaves a substantial quantitative gap. Their corrected 2015 version retains the binary theorem while withdrawing an erroneous multiclass extension.

A studied auxiliary question asks whether each class embeds in an extremal class of comparable VC dimension. Chase and coauthors show that such embeddings can require an exponential increase in dimension. Their COLT 2024 result rules out that general route to a linear bound; it does not show that the original class itself needs exponential compression. A failed intermediate representation is different from a lower bound against every compressor.

The problem also has concrete graph instances. Fix a graph and label sampled vertices according to membership in an unknown metric ball. Bourneuf and coauthors give proper schemes of size O(t log(t+1)) when the graph has treewidth at most t, and an analogous bound for cliquewidth. Proper means that decoding produces another ball, a stronger requirement than this card imposes. Their April 2026 work supplies structured examples and explicitly leaves the general linear-VC conjecture open.

Attias, Hanneke, and Ramaswami show how binary compression results transfer to multiclass, regression, and robust-learning settings, with additional factors or additional requirements on the binary scheme. Consequently, a solution could have consequences beyond binary prediction, but those transfers have hypotheses. In particular, their Open Problem 28 is about adversarially robust compression; the standard conjecture used here appears in their introduction.

cards.title: Polynomial-time learning parity with constant random noise
cards.formal: For every fixed rational noise rate η with 0<η<1/2, does there exist a uniform classical randomized polynomial-time algorithm that, for every n and every secret s∈{0,1}^n, recovers s with probability at least 2/3 from independent samples (a,⟨a,s⟩⊕e), where a is uniform in {0,1}^n and e is independently Bernoulli(η)?
cards.definitions: The inner product ⟨a,s⟩ is Σ_i a_i s_i modulo two, and ⊕ is addition modulo two. The unknown s is fixed throughout an execution. Each requested sample uses a fresh independent uniform vector a and an independent error bit e, with Pr[e=1]=η. The learner knows n and the fixed rate η, and receives only classical samples. It cannot choose a, request a noiseless label, identify which labels were corrupted, or make coherent quantum queries. For each fixed η the algorithm and its polynomial bound pη may depend on η, but they must be uniform in n, without advice. Every execution uses at most pη(n) bit operations and requests at most pη(n) samples; reading and storing samples is charged. Polynomially many stored bits and repeated access to stored samples are allowed. The success probability is over the example generator and the learner’s random coins, for each fixed s. The desired output is the entire secret vector, not merely a predictor with unspecified advantage. No sparsity promise is imposed on s or on a. The quantifier over fixed rational η does not demand a running-time bound uniform as η approaches 1/2 with n.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: A canonical computational learning problem where a tiny amount of independent label noise defeats the obvious algebraic method, connecting efficient learning, random-code decoding and cryptographic hardness.

context_blocks.text: A parity function is among the simplest algebraic classifiers: choose a hidden subset of coordinates and return their XOR. Without label noise, sufficiently many random examples give linear equations, and Gaussian elimination recovers the secret with high probability. Independent noise changes the task from solving a consistent system to identifying which apparent equations should be trusted. Ordinary elimination mixes error bits along with the equations, so its usual exactness argument no longer applies.

The difficulty is computational rather than a lack of information. For a fixed noise rate below one half, the true secret agrees with a fresh label with probability 1−η. Every other secret agrees with probability one half under the uniform distribution on inputs. With a sufficiently large constant multiple of n examples, concentration and a union bound over the 2^n candidates identify the true secret with high probability. Exhaustively testing those candidates takes exponential time, leaving open whether their search can be avoided.

At η=1/4, for example, the correct candidate has expected agreement 3/4, while every incorrect parity has expected agreement 1/2. A threshold strictly between these values separates them once enough independent samples have been collected. This simple gap explains why a polynomial sample bound alone is not the desired breakthrough. One must locate the exceptional candidate efficiently among exponentially many possibilities.

Writing the sample vectors as rows of a matrix A gives b=As+e over the binary field. The columns of A generate a random linear code, and the task becomes decoding a random noisy codeword. This connection explains the relevance to cryptography. It does not turn a worst-case NP-hardness theorem for decoding arbitrary codes into an average-case hardness theorem for the random distribution used here. Quantifiers over matrices, errors and sample counts have to survive the reduction.

Blum, Kalai and Wasserman give a 2^{O(n/log n)}-time algorithm using a comparable subexponential number of examples for constant noise. Combining examples cancels blocks of coordinates, while the analysis controls how the combined noise approaches a fair coin. Their work also separates noise-tolerant learning from the statistical-query framework in an appropriate restricted parity regime. Thus failure of statistical-query methods cannot simply be interpreted as failure of all algorithms with access to individual examples.

Lyubashevsky answers a different sample-efficiency question: subexponential computation is possible using only n^{1+ε} examples for each fixed ε>0. The resulting running time is 2^{O(n/log log n)}. This result is directly relevant to a learner that can collect only polynomially many samples, but its time bound is still superpolynomial. Keeping the two resources visible prevents the better exponent of the many-sample algorithm from being quoted as a polynomial-sample guarantee.

There are substantial unconditional lower bounds in restricted resource models. Garg, Kothari, Liu and Raz show that a streaming learner needs either Ω(n²/(1/2−η)) bits of memory or exponentially many samples, with a strong success-probability guarantee in their theorem. For fixed η, the memory alternative is quadratic, which is permitted by the polynomial-time question. This establishes a real storage cost without ruling out a general polynomial-time algorithm.

Aggarwal, Gupta and Zeyong’s May 2026 hardness amplification relates success on a small fraction of instances to success on almost all instances after changing the dimension and noise parameters. Aggarwal and coauthors’ September 8 revision gives low-noise LPN hardness under simultaneous worst-case assumptions concerning decoding a code and distinguishing noisy codewords of its dual. These strengthen the understanding of hardness assumptions; neither is an unconditional proof that this learner cannot exist.

The every-secret guarantee is not an artificial extra obstacle compared with a uniform random secret. A learner can choose a uniform mask r, replace each label b by b⊕⟨a,r⟩, learn the masked secret s⊕r and remove the mask. The transformed secret is uniform while the noise law is unchanged. The central uncertainty therefore persists even when randomness in the hidden parity itself is supplied for free.

cards.title: Learning Boolean juntas from uniform random examples
cards.formal: Does there exist a uniform randomized algorithm that learns every Boolean k-junta on n variables from independent uniform random labelled examples in time polynomial in n, 2^k and 1/ε, with uniform-distribution error at most ε and success probability at least 2/3?
cards.definitions: For integers 0≤k≤n, a k-junta is a function f:{0,1}ⁿ→{0,1} for which there is an unknown set S⊆{1,…,n}, |S|≤k, and an arbitrary Boolean function g on |S| bits such that f(x)=g(x restricted to S). The learner receives n,k and a positive integer t≥3, setting ε=1/t. Each requested example consists of an independently uniform x∈{0,1}ⁿ and its exact, noiseless label f(x). The learner may request further independent examples, but cannot choose inputs to be labelled or obtain correlated examples. The output is a finite Boolean circuit h on n input bits; it need not itself be a k-junta. With probability at least 2/3 over all examples and internal random bits, Pr over a fresh uniform x that h(x)≠f(x) is at most 1/t. One fixed classical probabilistic Turing machine must run, on every sample and random tape, for at most (n+2^k+t)^C steps, up to a fixed multiplicative constant, for a universal constant C independent of n,k,t,f. Reading examples, computation and writing the circuit count toward this bound. Restricting ε to reciprocal integers is equivalent, up to polynomial factors, to the usual arbitrary-accuracy requirement.

cards.why: Determine whether arbitrary dependence on a small hidden set of variables can be learned efficiently from ordinary observations, separating computational search from sample sufficiency.

importance.reason: A central unresolved task in computational learning theory, isolating feature selection and serving as a prerequisite for efficient learning of general decision trees and DNF formulas.
