cards.status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. The SODA 2026 connectivity paper explicitly retains deterministic polylogarithmic worst-case updates as open. Its unconditional new bound is randomized and expected; its deterministic polylogarithmic conclusion depends on the stated static low-congestion sparsifier construction. Deterministic subpolynomial worst-case bounds and polylogarithmic amortized bounds are already known.

context_blocks.text: The difficulty is deleting an edge that belongs to a maintained spanning forest. Removing it splits one tree into two parts, but the graph might still connect those parts through an edge outside the forest. The data structure must find such a replacement quickly or correctly certify that none exists. A single deletion can expose a large cut, so simply scanning all candidate edges gives no small bound on the time of that update.

Holm, de Lichtenberg and Thorup give deterministic O(log² n) amortized operation bounds for connectivity, using a hierarchy of forests and edge levels. Their result establishes that long update sequences can be processed efficiently. The accounting permits an individual deletion to spend work paid for by other operations. Guaranteeing low latency after every deletion requires more than redistributing the same amortized accounting on paper.

Kapron, King and Mountjoy obtain polylogarithmic worst-case update time with randomization and a small error probability. Their cutset sampling technique tries to isolate a remaining edge across a cut, which can then be recovered from a compact sketch. Failure to recover an edge may mean either that the cut is empty or that the random samples missed it. Eliminating this uncertainty while keeping every update fast is part of the deterministic challenge.

Chuzhoy and coauthors use deterministic balanced-cut machinery to achieve n^{o(1)} worst-case update time, removing the earlier polynomial barrier. This is a major improvement but still leaves the present target open. For example, exp(√log n) is smaller than every fixed positive power of n and larger than every fixed power of log n. Thus a subpolynomial theorem does not imply the polylogarithmic bound merely by choosing a small exponent.

Meierhans and Probst Gutenberg’s SODA 2026 algorithm is Las Vegas: it maintains a correct spanning forest and achieves polylogarithmic expected worst-case update time, even against an adaptive adversary with access to its state. It alternates vertex and edge sparsification in a hierarchy. Each graph update changes the output forest by at most two edges, so maintaining the explicit answer itself does not cause large update costs. The expectation remains a distinction from the deterministic target.

The same paper gives a concrete sufficient condition for derandomization. If a deterministic algorithm constructs a near-linear-edge subgraph together with paths routing the original edges through it in m·polylog(m) time, with congestion at most (m/n)·polylog(m), the framework yields deterministic polylogarithmic worst-case connectivity. Congestion counts how many routed paths use the busiest retained edge. Finding any spanning forest is insufficient: its tree edges may carry far too many such paths.

A companion SODA 2026 result by Meierhans, Probst Gutenberg and Saranurak controls both the time and the number of vertices removed when pruning an expander after one edge deletion. This avoids a large burst of changes propagating through a hierarchy. It is an ingredient in the recent randomized progress; it does not by itself supply the deterministic sparsifier construction needed for the full conclusion.

Known lower bounds do not rule out the target. Pătraşcu and Demaine prove logarithmic amortized cell-probe lower bounds, including for connectivity on disjoint paths. Those results show that dynamic connectivity already has a real information-transfer cost in very simple graphs, but a logarithmic barrier is compatible with polylogarithmic upper bounds. The open issue is whether exact connectivity, deterministic computation and a bound on every operation can be achieved simultaneously.

cards.title: Fully dynamic near-optimal matching with polylogarithmic updates
cards.formal: For every fixed rational ε∈(0,1), is there a randomized fully dynamic algorithm that maintains an explicit matching M with |M|≥ν(G)/(1+ε) in every current general graph G using polylogarithmic expected amortized update time against an oblivious adversary?
cards.definitions: The graph is simple, undirected and unweighted, on the fixed vertex set [n], n≥2; ν(G) is its maximum matching cardinality. It starts empty. An update inserts one absent edge or deletes one present edge. Updates arrive online, but the entire valid sequence is fixed independently of the algorithm’s random bits and is not revealed in advance. More precisely, for every fixed ε and constant a≥1, require constants K,d,B and a uniform randomized word-RAM algorithm A_{ε,a} such that every sequence of T≤n^a updates has expected total initialization-plus-update cost at most K[n+T(log₂(n+2))^d]. Words have B⌈log₂(n+2)⌉ bits; standard word operations, memory access and retained random bits are charged. With probability at least 1−n^{−3}, after every update in the sequence an explicit mate array represents a valid matching satisfying the approximation bound. Reading a vertex’s mate or the matching cardinality takes O(1) time; enumerating all matching edges costs O(n) and need not occur after every update. Changes to the mate array count toward update cost. Constants may depend on ε and a, but not on n, T or the sequence. No polynomial dependence on 1/ε, adaptive-adversary guarantee or worst-case per-update bound is required. The word instructions are random-access reads/writes, comparisons, conditional branches, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo 2^w, integer quotient/remainder with nonzero divisor, bitwise Boolean operations, and shifts of a w-bit word; shifts by at least w yield zero. The constant in word length w=Θ(log n) (or Θ(log N) when N is the stated input size) is fixed with the algorithm. Address arithmetic has the same cost, larger integers occupy multiple words, and no instruction performs arbitrary-precision arithmetic in one step. When randomization is allowed, a fresh independent uniform w-bit word costs one operation. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.

cards.status_note: Reviewed through 11 September 2026. No polylogarithmic-update algorithm meeting the fixed-accuracy, explicit-matching target was found. Matching-size estimators, ordered-RS-dependent bounds and the 2026 maximal-matching improvement do not resolve it.

context_blocks.text: A maximum matching allocates the largest possible number of disjoint pairs. When an edge changes, recomputing it from scratch ignores the substantial information retained from the preceding graph. The dynamic problem asks how much of that information can be reused while keeping a solution within an arbitrarily small fixed relative loss of optimum. Both insertions and deletions are allowed, so previously useful structure can disappear.

The graph’s optimum changes by at most one after a single edge update, but a particular solution may require coordinated replacements. On a long alternating path, gaining one additional matched edge can involve changing many pairs. Approximation creates room to postpone or distribute some repairs. The difficulty is to do so without accumulating a large loss or spending too much time discovering the repairs that are needed.

An explicit solution is part of the target. A number close to ν(G) need not identify even one edge that can safely be used with the others. A mate array makes this distinction observable: a query at a vertex must return its current partner or report that it is unmatched. Requiring the whole array to be printed after every update would impose an artificial linear output cost, so the formulation instead charges only actual changes and queries.

Maximality is also weaker than near-optimality. In a four-vertex path, selecting only the middle edge gives a maximal matching of size one, while the two outside edges give a maximum matching of size two. Randomized maximal-matching algorithms already achieve very small update times against oblivious sequences. Chuzhoy–Khanna–Song’s STOC 2026 result improves deterministic maximal matching to n^{1/2+o(1)} amortized time; its guarantee still concerns maximality.

A separate sequence of breakthroughs beats the factor-two barrier for estimating matching size in polylogarithmic update time. Azarmehr–Behnezhad–Roghani’s SODA 2024 result obtains an estimate corresponding to a 2−√2−η fraction of optimum in general graphs, for fixed η>0. The paper explicitly studies size estimation. Its title alone can therefore suggest a stronger maintenance result than the theorem actually supplies.

For maintaining actual near-optimal matchings, Assadi–Khanna–Kiss’s SODA 2025 work develops a connection to ordered Ruzsa–Szemerédi graphs. Such a graph has its edges partitioned into matchings, with each matching induced in the union of itself and later matchings. Dense examples quantify how often certain expensive matching searches can recur. Their update bound is expressed through this extremal quantity and works even against adaptive adversaries.

The dependence is roughly n^{o(1)} times the ordered-RS count for matchings of linear size, with accuracy-dependent parameters. A strong enough combinatorial upper bound would yield subpolynomial update time. This does not currently establish polylogarithmic time: n^{o(1)} can grow faster than every fixed power of log n, and the required extremal bounds are themselves unresolved. This connection is not an unconditional lower bound.

Pratt’s SOSA 2026 note relates the ordered and ordinary RS notions at the level of polynomial exponents. Dense ordered examples would imply nearly comparably dense ordinary examples. It resolves a structural question about the reduction’s graph families, but does not determine the density needed for a polylogarithmic dynamic algorithm.

Liu’s 2024 work gives a different advance for bipartite graphs: amortized update time n/2^{Ω(√log n)} times a polynomial in 1/ε. It also relates stronger update bounds to online matrix-vector problems. The dependence on accuracy is essential in those statements. In particular, the ordinary-OMv equivalence stated for approximate vertex cover should not be silently transferred to matching, and a barrier using inverse-polynomial accuracy does not settle this card’s fixed-ε question.

The adversary convention leaves useful flexibility. An oblivious sequence may be carefully chosen to be difficult, but it cannot react to random decisions or the current matching. The algorithm nevertheless receives updates one at a time; knowing that the sequence was fixed does not give access to future deletions. Similarly, amortization permits occasional expensive repairs as long as their expected total cost satisfies the bound.

The inherited Max Planck report explicitly identifies near-optimal fully dynamic matching with polylogarithmic updates as a long-term target. Its page 123 also distinguishes maintaining matching edges from estimating their number, and describes faster progress in the insertion-only setting. Allowing deletion of a vertex, which removes all its incident edges together, does not automatically supply an algorithm for arbitrary individual edge deletions.

The fundamental issue is whether a changing combinatorial optimum can be tracked almost as cheaply as the graph itself is updated. A positive result would close a major gap between coarse approximation and near-optimal explicit solutions. It would also clarify how much global matching structure must be recomputed when each input change is local.

cards.title: Polynomial-sample worst-case trace reconstruction
cards.formal: For every fixed deletion probability δ∈(0,1), is there a constant C_δ≥1 and K_δ≥1 such that every unknown n-bit string can be reconstructed exactly with probability at least 2/3 from at most K_δ n^{C_δ} independent deletion traces, for every n≥2?
cards.definitions: For x∈{0,1}^n, a deletion trace is generated by independently retaining each input bit with probability 1−δ and concatenating the retained bits in their original order. Let μ_{x,δ} be its probability distribution on ⋃_{k=0}^n{0,1}^k. Different traces use independent deletion masks. The estimator is given n, δ and m independent samples from μ_{x,δ}; it receives neither deletion positions nor direct access to x. Its output is an element of {0,1}^n, and success means equality to the entire original string. One estimator for the given n and δ must succeed for every x with probability at least 2/3 over the traces and any internal randomness. There is no restriction on processing time, storage, description length or computation between observations: this card asks an information-theoretic sample-complexity question. Formally, let N_δ(n) be the smallest integer m for which such an estimator exists. The target is N_δ(n)≤K_δ n^{C_δ} for every n≥2. The constants may depend on δ but not on n or x. The string is adversarially chosen and has no codebook, sparsity, separation, randomness or other structural promise. Traces are ordinary linear subsequences without cyclic shifts.

context_blocks.text: The input is one unknown string, observed repeatedly through independent losses of symbols. A surviving output bit carries its value but loses its original index. Repetition gives more evidence about the same underlying string, so the question is how many damaged copies contain enough information for exact recovery in the worst case.

There is an immediate exponential upper bound: with probability (1−δ)^n a trace suffers no deletions and reveals the entire string. After sufficiently many samples, such a length-n trace appears with high probability. The challenge is to extract the same information from much shorter typical traces without waiting for this rare event. Their lengths are observable, so the no-deletion event is recognizable.

Lower bounds can focus on two carefully selected strings whose trace distributions are extremely close. It improves the upper frontier considerably while still leaving a gap to a fixed polynomial in n.

The same paper explicitly separates sample complexity from running time. Maximum-likelihood reconstruction can reuse these traces while comparing exponentially many candidate strings, whereas distinguishing two supplied candidates can be implemented much faster. The quasipolynomial sample theorem does not provide quasipolynomial time for reconstructing an arbitrary unknown string. Since the current card imposes no time limit, this distinction does not weaken the sample result.

The change in statistics matters. A local statistical-query procedure learns only approximate expectations of functions inspecting a short consecutive block of trace positions. Chen and coauthors prove strong accuracy requirements for that model, nearly matching the older subexponential algorithm. Those lower bounds do not apply to unrestricted use of individual traces or to statistics involving widely separated positions. Thus the new global approach does not contradict the local-query barrier.

Structural promises can also make the problem easier. Their definition requires polylogarithmic separation. The theorem cannot be applied to arbitrary dense strings or to every constant deletion probability without additional arguments.

Circular trace reconstruction adds an unknown cyclic shift to each observation and asks for recovery up to rotation. The 2026 circular lower bound of roughly n⁵ is consequently a theorem for a different observation model. It should not replace the linear-model lower bound in this card. Likewise, deletion-channel coding permits a chosen codebook, while the worst-case reconstruction requirement here must cover every binary string.

cards.title: Constant-factor edit-distance approximation in O(n polylog n) time
cards.formal: Do absolute constants C≥1, K>0 and d≥0 and a uniform randomized classical algorithm exist that, for every two length-n strings x,y, output an integer D satisfying ED(x,y)≤D≤C·ED(x,y) with probability at least 2/3 in at most Kn(log₂(n+2))^d time?
cards.definitions: Use the unit-cost Levenshtein distance: ED is the minimum number of single-symbol insertions, deletions and substitutions transforming x into y; matching equal symbols costs zero. The input consists of n≥1 and two explicitly stored arrays x,y∈{0,…,n²+1}ⁿ. This fixes an integer alphabet whose symbols fit in O(log n) bits and includes binary and fixed finite alphabets. Computation is on a word RAM with word length B⌈log₂(n+2)⌉ for an absolute constant B, using random access, comparisons, Boolean operations, shifts and word arithmetic at unit cost. The algorithm may draw independent random bits, but has no input-dependent advice, preprocessed database or oracle. All preprocessing counts toward the bound, which must hold on every execution. Success is required separately for every input pair. Output only the distance estimate; an edit script is not required. The constants C,K,d,B are fixed independently of n and the strings. There is no promise about the distance, repetitions or input distribution, and no additive error is allowed. The word instructions are random-access reads/writes, comparisons, conditional branches, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo 2^w, integer quotient/remainder with nonzero divisor, bitwise Boolean operations, and shifts of a w-bit word; shifts by at least w yield zero. The constant in word length w=Θ(log n) (or Θ(log N) when N is the stated input size) is fixed with the algorithm. Address arithmetic has the same cost, larger integers occupy multiple words, and no instruction performs arbitrary-precision arithmetic in one step. When randomization is allowed, a fresh independent uniform w-bit word costs one operation. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.

cards.status_note: Reviewed through 11 September 2026. No O(n polylog n)-time, fixed-constant approximation for all input pairs was found in the checked primary sources. context_blocks.text: Insertions and deletions make alignment the central difficulty. If a symbol is inserted near the start of a string, many later positions shift, even when almost all symbols are unchanged. Comparing corresponding positions can therefore report many mismatches while a short edit sequence exists. The task is to estimate the best alignment cost without inspecting the full quadratic dynamic-programming table.

For example, deleting the first symbol of an alternating binary string and reinserting it at the end produces an equal-length string with almost every position changed, but edit distance at most two. A Hamming-distance estimate can be linear in the length on this pair. This illustrates why a simple positional comparison cannot provide a universal constant-factor approximation.

The multiplicative guarantee is deliberately strict at small distances. When x=y, success requires D=0. When the true distance is one, the returned value must remain bounded by the same universal C used on arbitrarily long strings. An additive error such as n^{0.9} can be acceptable for very distant strings while being arbitrarily poor on these nearby pairs. Reading both complete strings is allowed; this is not a sublinear-query problem.

Early algorithms already showed that one could gain substantial speed by allowing larger distortion. Andoni–Onak obtain a subpolynomial approximation factor 2^{Õ(√log n)} in n^{1+o(1)} time, with a STOC 2009 precursor and a later journal version. Both quantities improve substantially on older polynomial approximations, but the factor still grows with input length.

Koucký–Saks obtain a constant-factor result for sufficiently distant pairs, with an additive n^{1−ζ} term in the general guarantee. The exponent ζ and the multiplicative constant depend on the fixed runtime parameter. Their theorem makes the missing regime explicit: the additive term cannot be absorbed into a constant times the true distance on every pair.

Andoni–Nosatzki remove that distance promise. Their Theorem 1.1 gives, for every fixed ε>0, an O(n^{1+ε})-time randomized algorithm with approximation f(1/ε). The manuscript notes doubly exponential dependence on 1/ε. Its FOCS 2020 result was revised on arXiv in July 2022 and published in SIAM Journal on Computing in August 2026. The recent publication date does not change the quantified n^{1+ε} guarantee into n times a polylogarithm.

The order of these choices is decisive. A fixed ε=0.01 gives a fixed approximation factor, but n^{0.01} eventually exceeds every fixed power of log n. Choosing ε as a function of n to force the desired runtime also changes the approximation factor and the hidden constants. The theorem does not provide the single constant C required here. This is a quantitative gap within already very fast approximation algorithms, rather than a question about whether any strongly subquadratic constant approximation exists.

Mao–Rubinstein’s STOC 2026 work improves a different part of the tradeoff. For every fixed accuracy parameter η>0, it gives a randomized (1+η)-approximation in n²/2^{log^{Ω(1)}n} time. The approximation can be arbitrarily close to exact, but the displayed speedup is over the quadratic scale, not down to n polylog n. It does not resolve this card’s constant-factor, much-faster-runtime target.

Backurs–Indyk’s SETH-based barrier concerns exact computation in strongly subquadratic time. It should not be applied indiscriminately to approximation: the known constant-factor algorithms already run in that regime. An impossibility result for the present question would need to preserve a multiplicative gap of the appropriate size while respecting the randomized model and the very small runtime overhead.

The card concerns ordinary strings and numerical estimation. Tree edit distance, distances between languages, weighted edit operations and quantum algorithms each change the problem. Likewise, an efficient nearest-neighbour data structure with substantial preprocessing does not immediately yield the stated two-string algorithm. These distinctions keep the target useful as a precise benchmark for the algorithmic complexity of a basic sequence metric.

A positive resolution would show that constant distortion suffices to reduce this alignment problem to essentially the cost of reading its input, up to logarithmic factors. Even a large universal approximation constant would settle that structural issue. Reducing the constant, producing an alignment, and obtaining practical implementations would remain meaningful subsequent goals.

The separate card TCS-7220 asks whether every fixed ε>0 permits a (1+ε)-approximation in O(n^(2−δ_ε)) time for some fixed δ_ε>0. Its near-exact guarantee does not by itself provide this card’s O(n polylog n) runtime, while this card’s unspecified constant factor does not supply arbitrary 1+ε accuracy. The user explicitly approved retaining both targets on 11 September 2026.

cards.title: Constant-factor universally truthful auctions for submodular bidders
cards.area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
cards.formal: Does there exist a universal constant C≥1 and a randomized, universally truthful combinatorial-auction mechanism that, for every number n of bidders, number m of items and normalized monotone submodular valuation profile, uses polynomial communication and produces an allocation of expected social welfare at least OPT/C?
cards.definitions: There are m≥1 distinct indivisible items and n≥1 bidders. Bidder i privately knows v_i:2^[m]→Q_{≥0}, with v_i(∅)=0, v_i(S)≤v_i(T) for S⊆T, and v_i(S)+v_i(T)≥v_i(S∪T)+v_i(S∩T) for all S,T. To make communication in bits precise, a public integer B≥1 bounds the binary lengths of the numerator and positive denominator of each value. This is a bound per value, not permission to transmit the exponential table. One uniform protocol must work for every n,m,B with at most P(n,m,B) communicated bits in the worst case, for one fixed polynomial P. Arbitrary interactive messages and demand queries are allowed; all query descriptions, replies, allocations and payments count toward communication. Local computation by bidders and auctioneer is unrestricted but must terminate. An outcome consists of pairwise disjoint bundles S_1,…,S_n and rational payments p_1,…,p_n; unallocated items are allowed. Utilities are quasilinear, u_i=v_i(S_i)−p_i. There are no private budgets or distributional assumptions. Universal truthfulness means the mechanism is a report-independent distribution over deterministic dominant-strategy truthful mechanisms: for every fixed random seed r, every i, every admissible true and alternative reported type v_i,v_i′, and every v_{−i}, v_i(S_i(v_i,v_{−i};r))−p_i(v_i,v_{−i};r)≥v_i(S_i(v_i′,v_{−i};r))−p_i(v_i′,v_{−i};r). A low-communication protocol implements this outcome and payment rule on the distributed reported types. OPT=max Σ_i v_i(T_i), where the maximum is over pairwise disjoint T_i⊆[m]. The expected welfare guarantee holds for every truthful valuation profile, with expectation only over the mechanism’s randomness; C is independent of n,m,B. No additional individual-rationality or transfer-sign restriction is imposed in this formulation.

cards.why: Determine whether exact truthful incentives inherently cause an unbounded loss of allocative efficiency, even when arbitrary compact communication and unlimited local optimization are available.

importance.reason: A central multi-parameter mechanism-design problem linking truthful incentives, submodular optimization, information elicitation and the communication cost of welfare approximation.

cards.status_note: The checked primary literature retains a gap between constant nontruthful welfare approximation and the general universally truthful guarantee. Theorem 2 of the SODA 2021 paper supplies O((log log m)²) for submodular bidders. The 2026 graph-auction results impose eligibility restrictions. No general constant-factor resolution found through 11 September 2026. The public per-value precision parameter makes the inherited polynomial-communication question explicit in bits.

context_blocks.text: A bidder may value several items as substitutes. For example, a coverage valuation assigns each item a set of useful features and values a bundle by the total weight of features covered at least once. Receiving an item has less marginal value when many of its features are already covered. Submodularity abstracts this diminishing-returns property without requiring the valuation to be supplied as an explicit coverage instance.

The auctioneer must allocate the items using information held by strategic bidders. Maximizing the sum of their values is the social-welfare objective; maximizing the auctioneer’s revenue would be a different problem. Payments influence what information bidders choose to provide, but are transfers and do not enter the welfare objective. Even a very poor revenue guarantee would be acceptable here if incentives and welfare met the stated requirements.

Two established results cover separate parts of the requirements. With complete reports and unrestricted resources, the Vickrey–Clarke–Groves mechanism obtains optimal welfare and truthful incentives. If incentives are omitted, submodular welfare admits constant-factor approximation from compact queries. The difficulty is combining the guarantees while avoiding communication of exponentially many bundle values. The 2026 graph-auctions paper describes this communication perspective explicitly.

Universal truthfulness is a strong use of randomization: each mechanism obtained after fixing the coins must itself make truthful reporting optimal. Truthfulness in expectation requires only that the average utility discourage lying. The distinction has mathematical force; Dobzinski and Dughmi separate the two notions in a restricted multi-unit setting. Their separation is useful background, but their multi-unit approximation scheme does not supply a mechanism for arbitrary heterogeneous submodular valuations.

A demand query offers item prices and asks a bidder to choose a bundle maximizing its value minus its total price. Sending that bundle requires only m membership bits, even when finding it takes enormous local computation. This is why allowing demand queries changes the problem substantially. The formulation deliberately measures communication: an algorithm that delegates difficult optimization to a bidder can qualify. It would need further work to become computationally efficient for that bidder.

Dobzinski’s impossibility theorem rules out universally truthful m^{1/2−ε}-approximation using polynomially many value queries, for every fixed ε>0. A value query reveals only one specified bundle’s value. The theorem is a genuine barrier in that access model, but it cannot be extended by simply treating a demand query as one more value query. A demand answer can encode the result of comparing exponentially many bundles.

Assadi and Singla reached an expected O((log log m)³) approximation using O(n) demand queries, at FOCS 2019. Assadi, Kesselheim and Singla subsequently improved the submodular guarantee to O((log log m)²), while obtaining O((log log m)³) for the broader subadditive class. These asymptotic factors grow with the number of items, despite growing very slowly.

The latter mechanism learns approximate item prices through random groups of bidders. A bidder participates in a single fixed-price auction, so its own report cannot manipulate the menu it faces. Some price-learning rounds can become the final allocation rather than merely gathering information; the analysis accounts for welfare earned in those rounds. This makes price discovery compatible with truthfulness, but leaves a loss between the learned allocation and optimal welfare.

Recent positive results for graph auctions restrict each item to a small set of eligible bidders. For example, the 2026 paper gives a truthful factor-two mechanism when each item has two eligible bidders and valuations are subadditive. This structural restriction supplies information absent in a general auction, so it does not settle the present question. A general constant-factor mechanism would show that exact incentive compatibility need not impose an unbounded welfare loss in this central communication model.

Receiving an item has less marginal value when many of its features are already covered. Submodularity abstracts this diminishing-returns property without requiring the valuation to be supplied as an explicit coverage instance.

The auctioneer must allocate the items using information held by strategic bidders. Maximizing the sum of their values is the social-welfare objective; maximizing the auctioneer’s revenue would be a different problem. Payments influence what information bidders choose to provide, but are transfers and do not enter the welfare objective. Even a very poor revenue guarantee would be acceptable here if incentives and welfare met the stated requirements.

Two established results cover separate parts of the requirements. With complete reports and unrestricted resources, the Vickrey–Clarke–Groves mechanism obtains optimal welfare and truthful incentives. If incentives are omitted, submodular welfare admits constant-factor approximation from compact queries. The difficulty is combining the guarantees while avoiding communication of exponentially many bundle values. The 2026 graph-auctions paper describes this communication perspective explicitly.

Universal truthfulness is a strong use of randomization: each mechanism obtained after fixing the coins must itself make truthful reporting optimal. Truthfulness in expectation requires only that the average utility discourage lying. The distinction has mathematical force; Dobzinski and Dughmi separate the two notions in a restricted multi-unit setting. Their separation is useful background, but their multi-unit approximation scheme does not supply a mechanism for arbitrary heterogeneous submodular valuations.

A demand query offers item prices and asks a bidder to choose a bundle maximizing its value minus its total price. Sending that bundle requires only m membership bits, even when finding it takes enormous local computation. This is why allowing demand queries changes the problem substantially. The formulation deliberately measures communication: an algorithm that delegates difficult optimization to a bidder can qualify. It would need further work to become computationally efficient for that bidder.

Dobzinski’s impossibility theorem rules out universally truthful m^{1/2−ε}-approximation using polynomially many value queries, for every fixed ε>0. A value query reveals only one specified bundle’s value. The theorem is a genuine barrier in that access model, but it cannot be extended by simply treating a demand query as one more value query. A demand answer can encode the result of comparing exponentially many bundles.

Assadi and Singla reached an expected O((log log m)³) approximation using O(n) demand queries, at FOCS 2019. Assadi, Kesselheim and Singla subsequently improved the submodular guarantee to O((log log m)²), while obtaining O((log log m)³) for the broader subadditive class. These asymptotic factors grow with the number of items, despite growing very slowly.

The latter mechanism learns approximate item prices through random groups of bidders. A bidder participates in a single fixed-price auction, so its own report cannot manipulate the menu it faces. Some price-learning rounds can become the final allocation rather than merely gathering information; the analysis accounts for welfare earned in those rounds. This makes price discovery compatible with truthfulness, but leaves a loss between the learned allocation and optimal welfare.

Recent positive results for graph auctions restrict each item to a small set of eligible bidders. For example, the 2026 paper gives a truthful factor-two mechanism when each item has two eligible bidders and valuations are subadditive. This structural restriction supplies information absent in a general auction, so it does not settle the present question. A general constant-factor mechanism would show that exact incentive compatibility need not impose an unbounded welfare loss in this central communication model.

cards.definitions: There are n agents and m indivisible goods, with [0]=∅. Agent i values a bundle S by v_i(S)=Σ_{g∈S}v_ig; values are finite, nonnegative real numbers. A partition consists of pairwise disjoint bundles whose union is all goods; empty bundles are allowed. Every good must be allocated exactly once. There are no payments, chores, probabilistic allocations or discarded goods. The displayed condition is envy-freeness up to any positively valued good (EFX): the removed good is tested using the values of agent i, not those of agent j. If v_i is zero on all of A_j, there is no inequality to check for that pair. This fixes the EFX convention of Definition 5 and Open Problem 2 of the cited survey. No algorithm, runtime, or restriction to rational or strictly positive values is required.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that every valuation matrix in the statement admits such a complete partition, or give an instance with n≥4 and finite m for which no complete partition satisfies all the EFX inequalities. The target concerns existence with nonnegative additive values; neither efficient computation nor any stronger fairness or efficiency property is required.

context_blocks.text: Indivisibility prevents ordinary envy-freeness even in the smallest examples. If four people all value a single good at one, whoever receives it is envied by the others. The allocation nevertheless satisfies EFX: removing that good leaves an empty bundle. EFX permits this unavoidable envy while limiting envy that survives the removal of any positively valued item. The removal is a hypothetical comparison; the actual allocation still assigns every good.

The word “any” makes the guarantee demanding. Suppose an agent values her own bundle at 4 and another bundle’s two goods at 6 and 1. Removing the 6-valued good eliminates her envy, so this pair satisfies the weaker EF1 test. Removing the 1-valued good leaves value 6, so this pair violates EFX. All comparisons use the potentially envious agent’s values, which can differ from the recipient’s.

Zero values require a convention. If an agent has value zero for her own bundle and values the goods in another bundle at 1 and 0, removing the positively valued good passes this card’s test. Requiring removal of the zero-valued good to pass as well would fail. That stronger condition on an individual allocation is often called EFX₀. The problem statement retains the survey’s positive-good EFX convention.

For three additive agents, Chaudhury, Garg and Mehlhorn prove complete EFX existence for any number of goods. Thus the universal question starts at four agents; it is the unrestricted number of goods at that first unresolved agent count that already presents a difficulty.

The four-agent theorem of Berger, Cohen, Feldman and Fiat leaves at most one good unassigned. Completeness matters: adding that final good can create new envy, so an almost complete allocation does not itself answer the stated question.

In August 2026, Alkassar, Fouz and Mehlhorn reported complete EFX₀ existence for four agents and at most nine goods, allowing arbitrary nonnegative real values. Their theorem uses reductions and a computational certificate corpus. EFX₀ implies the EFX condition here, but the bounded number of goods leaves the unrestricted target open. The theorem’s stated scope was checked; its computations were not rerun.

Recent nonexistence results concern broader valuation classes. Mackenzie and Suzuki give counterexamples with submodular and subadditive valuations, where the value of a bundle need not equal the sum of its individual goods’ values. Such examples do not meet the additive hypothesis on this card. Likewise, a chores result concerns unwanted items and a different fairness comparison.

The issue is existence for every input valuation matrix, without an efficiency requirement. An affirmative theorem would guarantee a complete allocation with this strong relaxation of envy-freeness. A negative answer needs one additive instance in the stated domain for which every complete partition fails; finding a poor allocation or a failing allocation algorithm is insufficient.

cards.title: Is the matrix multiplication exponent equal to two?
cards.formal: Fix the field of complex numbers. Let s(n) be the minimum number of arithmetic gates in a circuit that computes all entries of AB exactly for arbitrary n-by-n matrices A,B. Is it true that $\forall\varepsilon>0\;\exists C_\varepsilon>0\;\forall n\ge2:\ s(n)\le C_\varepsilon n^{2+\varepsilon}$? Equivalently, is $\omega=\inf\{\tau:s(n)=O(n^\tau)\}=2$?
cards.definitions: The inputs are 2n² independent complex variables a_ij,b_ij. The required n² output polynomials are c_ij=sum_{k=1}^n a_ik b_kj. A circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph with binary addition, subtraction, and multiplication gates; any complex constants and unrestricted reuse of intermediate values are allowed. Size counts arithmetic gates, including operations involving constants. Input nodes, constant nodes, and output designations are not gates. No division, order comparisons, branching, approximation, or randomization is permitted. A different circuit may be chosen for every n: this is the standard nonuniform arithmetic-complexity formulation over C. The cost of encoding a complex number in bits is outside this model. The elementary lower bound s(n)>=n² for n>=2 follows because the n² distinct non-input output polynomials require distinct gates.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: Matrix multiplication is a basic operation whose exponent enters many algorithms in linear algebra and graph theory. Determining whether its arithmetic cost can approach the quadratic scale would settle a central question about sharing computation among many related outputs.

importance.reason: One of the main questions in algebraic algorithms, governing a widely used primitive and many dependent complexity bounds. Both faster constructions and a superquadratic lower bound would have broad consequences.

progress.text: Strassen gives O(n^(log₂7)) arithmetic operations, establishing that cubic multiplication is not optimal.

Alman proves that the universal method applied to any Coppersmith–Winograd tensor cannot yield an exponent below 2.16805. This is a limitation of that tensor-based route, not a proof that omega exceeds two.
The SODA paper More Asymmetry Yields Faster Matrix Multiplication gives omega<2.371339 by extending the combination-loss analysis. The original preprint appeared in April 2024.

Dupont and coauthors report omega<2.371177. Section 4 describes rounding the optimized parameters to rationals and verifying directed bounds for logarithms; it says the verification repository is being prepared. This catalogue has not independently replayed that certificate.
Version 3 of More Asymmetry Yields Faster Matrix Multiplication incorporates the new optimization bound. The remaining gap to two persists.

cards.status_note: The latest primary upper bound located through 10 September 2026 is the reported omega<2.371177 from August 2026. It leaves the omega=2 question open. The model is exact arithmetic over C; the catalogue has not independently reproduced the numerical certificate.

context_blocks.text: The usual algorithm computes n² inner products of length n, spending cubic arithmetic work. That computation treats the outputs separately even though they share their input matrices. Strassen’s construction shows that this shared structure can save an asymptotic factor: seven block multiplications replace eight in a two-by-two block product, and recursive use gives exponent log₂7.

The question is whether one can keep reducing the extra exponent all the way to zero. Its quantifiers matter. An algorithm for each exponent 2+epsilon is enough, even when its constant depends badly on epsilon. Conversely, improving one decimal place in the current upper bound does not establish the conjecture. Fixing the field and counting exact scalar operations also separates this question from approximate numerical multiplication or hardware throughput.

Modern upper bounds encode multiplication in tensors and exploit savings across large tensor powers. A substantial part of their analysis can be expressed as an optimization over parameters. The August 2026 improvement expands that optimization and uses new search procedures to find better parameters; the paper then describes rational verification of the resulting inequalities. That is an arithmetic exponent result, not an empirical speed comparison.

There are also lower bounds on what specific tensor methods can achieve. For example, Alman’s universal-method barrier for Coppersmith–Winograd tensors prevents that route from reaching exponent two. It is not a lower bound on all arithmetic circuits for matrix multiplication. The distinction leaves room for different starting tensors or mathematical constructions.

cards.title: Does the permanent require determinants of superpolynomial dimension?
cards.formal: Over the complex numbers, is the sequence dc_C(permₙ) unbounded by every polynomial in n? Explicitly, for every C>0 and integer k≥1, must there be n≥1 such that dc_C(permₙ)>C(n+1)^k?
cards.definitions: The polynomial permₙ(X)=Σ_{σ∈Sₙ}∏_{i=1}ⁿx_{i,σ(i)} has n² algebraically independent commuting variables and degree n; Sₙ is the set of permutations of {1,…,n}. Its determinantal complexity dc_C(permₙ) is the smallest positive integer m for which there exist constant complex m×m matrices A₀ and Aᵢⱼ satisfying the exact polynomial identity permₙ(X)=det(A₀+Σ_{i,j=1}ⁿxᵢⱼAᵢⱼ). Thus every matrix entry is an arbitrary affine-linear form in all input variables. The representation may depend on n and use arbitrary complex constants without a bit-length or constructibility restriction. The resource is matrix dimension m. No symmetry, sparsity, multilinearity of intermediate expressions, regularity, or read-once restriction is imposed. Equality is in C[X], for every complex substitution, not only on 0/1 inputs. Border complexity, which permits a limit of representations, is a separate measure. Characteristic two is excluded by fixing C: in that characteristic the permanent equals the determinant. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: A central concrete target in algebraic complexity: determine whether one canonical efficiently computable polynomial can simulate a canonical algebraic counting polynomial at polynomial cost. Its formulation invites tools from algebraic geometry and representation theory while retaining a precise computational meaning.

importance.reason: The principal permanent-versus-determinant lower-bound problem, connecting algebraic computation, branching programs, geometry, and symmetry.

progress.text: Valiant establishes the foundational algebraic simulation framework: formulas and branching programs have small determinantal representations, and the permanent is complete for VNP.
Mignon and Ressayre prove dc_C(permₙ)≥n²/2 using Hessian ranks at zeros. This remains a polynomial lower bound.

Grenet gives a 2ⁿ−1-dimensional representation; Landsberg and Ressayre prove exponential optimality when specified symmetries must be respected. Their unrestricted-versus-equivariant comparison is left open.
Kumar and Volk survey the permanent bounds and develop a new singular-locus method for a different explicit polynomial, a diagonal power sum. That theorem does not raise the permanent lower bound.
The algebraic cost of Boolean summation distinguishes permanent and determinant under a local fixed-additive-size simulation requirement, leaving general polynomial-size representations open.
Bogart and Valero’s journal paper studies generalized permanents and continues to state the superpolynomial ordinary-permanent problem as open.

cards.status_note: Open in the cited foundational and recent papers; checked through 10 September 2026. This card fixes exact unrestricted representations over C. Symmetric, equivariant, real-field, border, and other-polynomial bounds are not substituted for this model.

context_blocks.text: The permanent and determinant sum the same products indexed by permutations; the determinant attaches a permutation sign. Those signs enable cancellations behind efficient determinant computation. A determinantal representation asks whether a larger matrix with carefully chosen affine entries can reproduce the unsigned sum exactly. Merely showing that changing signs in the original n×n matrix fails leaves almost all permitted representations untouched.

The model is nonuniform and algebraic. It asks about the existence of a family of polynomial-size representations even if finding their complex coefficients is computationally difficult. Determinants characterize polynomial-size algebraic branching programs up to polynomial overhead, whereas unrestricted arithmetic circuits define the potentially larger class VP. The requested lower bound separates the permanent from the branching-program model; it should not be identified without qualification with a separation from all of VP.

The unrestricted complex-field lower bound is still quadratic in the original matrix dimension: Mignon and Ressayre prove dc_C(permₙ)≥n²/2. Their argument compares the rank of the matrix of second partial derivatives, the Hessian, at carefully chosen zeros of the two polynomials. Because the permanent has n² input variables, this is only linear in its number of variables, despite being quadratic in n.

There is also an explicit exponential upper bound, dc_C(permₙ)≤2ⁿ−1, due to Grenet. Landsberg and Ressayre prove that this construction is optimal under particular equivariance requirements involving permutations and diagonal rescaling. Removing those requirements is essential: the question allows a representation to break every visible symmetry of the polynomial. Whether symmetry can be imposed with only polynomial overhead is itself another open problem.

Progress can reveal structural differences without giving an unrestricted lower bound. Orzel, Srinivasan, Tavenas, and Yehudayoff show that a local Boolean-summation operation can be absorbed into a permanent by a fixed additive increase in dimension, whereas the analogous uniform fixed-additive-cost property fails for determinants. Their FSTTCS 2025 result explains a step in the VNP-completeness construction; it does not exclude a different, global polynomial-size determinant representation.

Bogart and Valero extend upper- and lower-bound techniques to two generalized permanent families. Their 2026 journal version still identifies the Mignon–Ressayre estimate as the best known characteristic-zero bound for the ordinary permanent for n≥5. This provides a recent status check while illustrating how sensitive the geometric lower-bound method is to the polynomial being studied.

The permanent and determinant sum the same products indexed by permutations; the determinant attaches a permutation sign. Those signs enable cancellations behind efficient determinant computation. A determinantal representation asks whether a larger matrix with carefully chosen affine entries can reproduce the unsigned sum exactly. Merely showing that changing signs in the original n×n matrix fails leaves almost all permitted representations untouched.

The model is nonuniform and algebraic. It asks about the existence of a family of polynomial-size representations even if finding their complex coefficients is computationally difficult. Determinants characterize polynomial-size algebraic branching programs up to polynomial overhead, whereas unrestricted arithmetic circuits define the potentially larger class VP. The requested lower bound separates the permanent from the branching-program model; it should not be identified without qualification with a separation from all of VP.

The unrestricted complex-field lower bound is still quadratic in the original matrix dimension: Mignon and Ressayre prove dc_C(permₙ)≥n²/2. Their argument compares the rank of the matrix of second partial derivatives, the Hessian, at carefully chosen zeros of the two polynomials. Because the permanent has n² input variables, this is only linear in its number of variables, despite being quadratic in n.

There is also an explicit exponential upper bound, dc_C(permₙ)≤2ⁿ−1, due to Grenet. Landsberg and Ressayre prove that this construction is optimal under particular equivariance requirements involving permutations and diagonal rescaling. Removing those requirements is essential: the question allows a representation to break every visible symmetry of the polynomial. Whether symmetry can be imposed with only polynomial overhead is itself another open problem.

Progress can reveal structural differences without giving an unrestricted lower bound. Orzel, Srinivasan, Tavenas, and Yehudayoff show that a local Boolean-summation operation can be absorbed into a permanent by a fixed additive increase in dimension, whereas the analogous uniform fixed-additive-cost property fails for determinants. Their FSTTCS 2025 result explains a step in the VNP-completeness construction; it does not exclude a different, global polynomial-size determinant representation.

Bogart and Valero extend upper- and lower-bound techniques to two generalized permanent families. Their 2026 journal version still identifies the Mignon–Ressayre estimate as the best known characteristic-zero bound for the ordinary permanent for n≥5. This provides a recent status check while illustrating how sensitive the geometric lower-bound method is to the polynomial being studied.

benchmark_focus.reason: The principal permanent-versus-determinant lower-bound problem, connecting algebraic computation, branching programs, geometry, and symmetry.

cards.title: Is rational solvability of polynomial equations decidable?
cards.formal: Does there exist a Turing machine that, given any integer-coefficient polynomial f(X₁,…,Xₘ), always halts and correctly decides whether $\exists (q_1,\ldots,q_m)\in\mathbb Q^m:f(q_1,\ldots,q_m)=0$? The number of variables and polynomial degree are unrestricted parts of the finite input.
cards.definitions: Encode m≥1 and a finite list of monomials, each with a signed binary integer coefficient and an m-tuple of nonnegative binary exponents. Repeated monomials may be combined effectively; zero polynomials are allowed. A rational solution consists of exact fractions qᵢ=aᵢ/bᵢ, where aᵢ∈ℤ and bᵢ is a positive integer, with no prescribed bound on numerators or denominators. The required algorithm is one finite deterministic program, independent of m, degree, and coefficients. It must return yes exactly when a rational zero exists and no otherwise; it may use any finite amount of time and space on each input. Malformed encodings are rejected. The task supplies no oracle, height inequalities, integrality constraints on the unknowns, or promise of a solution. Rational coefficients would give an equivalent problem by clearing coefficient denominators. A finite system f₁=⋯=fᵣ=0 is equivalent over ℚ to the single equation f₁²+⋯+fᵣ²=0.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: This is a fundamental boundary between algorithmic arithmetic and undecidability. It asks whether exact rational polynomial constraints admit any general terminating solver, connecting computation, logical definability, and the arithmetic geometry of rational points.

importance.reason: A central unsolved decidability problem for an elementary, pervasive constraint language. A resolution would locate the computability boundary for rational polynomial feasibility.

progress.text: The Davis–Putnam–Robinson–Matiyasevich theorem settles the integer-solution problem negatively. The rational-solution analogue remains distinct.
Koenigsmann gives a universal first-order definition of ℤ in ℚ and related low-quantifier undecidability results. This does not supply an existential definition.
Anscombe and coauthors survey local-global methods and explicitly identify Hilbert’s tenth problem over number fields, including ℚ, as open.
Garcia-Fritz, Pasten, and Vidaux prove undecidability after adjoining finitely many height-comparison conditions. Those extra conditions are not part of ordinary rational solvability.

Rank-stability advances imply undecidability over rings of integers of all number fields. Poonen’s account dated 3 July 2026 reviews the proof and gives an alternative Diophantine-definability argument; the domains remain rings of integers.

context_blocks.text: Rational tuples can be enumerated by increasing bounds on their numerators and denominators, and substitution into an integer polynomial is exact and computable. Thus yes-instances can already be recognized eventually. The difficulty is knowing when to stop searching and certify that no rational point exists. The question asks about computability itself, before any requirement of efficiency.

Hilbert’s original problem required integer solutions. Matiyasevich’s completion of the Davis–Putnam–Robinson program proves that version undecidable. Permitting fractions changes the problem: a polynomial can have a rational zero and no integer zero, so applying a rational solver directly to the same equation would not decide the integer problem. A reduction must encode the missing integrality restriction using only the allowed rational polynomial equations.

An existential definition of ℤ inside ℚ would provide such an encoding and imply undecidability. Koenigsmann instead gives a universal definition of the integers, which is a major advance in definability but uses a different quantifier form. The full first-order theory of ℚ is already undecidable; the unresolved target concerns its existential fragment.

Recent results settle the analogous problem over the ring of integers of every number field. A ring of integers restricts denominators; it is not the whole number field. In particular the ring of integers of ℚ is ℤ, so this breakthrough does not decide the question on this card. Poonen’s July 2026 account explains how rank stability of abelian varieties yields the required Diophantine definitions for those rings.

Other nearby formulations add conditions comparing heights of rational coordinates. Garcia-Fritz, Pasten, and Vidaux prove an undecidability result with finitely many such conditions. Their formulation includes predicates absent here, and their paper explicitly retains ordinary Hilbert’s tenth problem over ℚ as open. This distinction matters when interpreting a result whose title refers to undecidable effectivity for rational points.

cards.title: Polynomial-time, polynomial-factor approximation of Euclidean SVP
cards.formal: Does there exist a constant C>0 and a classical randomized algorithm A running in polynomial time such that, for every rank-n rational lattice basis B, A outputs a nonzero integer vector z satisfying ∥Bz∥₂≤n^C λ₁(L(B)) with probability at least 2/3?
cards.definitions: The input is an explicitly encoded matrix B∈ℚ^{d×n}, d≥n≥1, with linearly independent columns. Each rational entry is given by a binary numerator and positive binary denominator. L(B)={Bz:z∈ℤⁿ} is the lattice, and λ₁(L)=min{∥v∥₂:0≠v∈L} is the length of a shortest nonzero vector in the Euclidean norm ∥v∥₂=(Σᵢvᵢ²)^{1/2}. Rank n, rather than ambient dimension d or coefficient magnitude, controls the approximation factor. There must be one polynomial P such that every run halts in at most P(L) bit operations, where L is the input’s total bit length; output bits and random bits are counted. Randomness consists of independent fair bits. Require z to be a nonzero integer vector on every run, while the length guarantee may fail with probability at most 1/3. Both P and C are independent of all input parameters. There are no distributional, uniqueness, conditioning, ideal-lattice or basis-quality promises. A deterministic algorithm would also qualify. The one-dimensional case is exactly solvable by a basis vector. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: A central algorithmic gap in lattice complexity: known polynomial-time methods give superpolynomial approximation factors, while key computational and cryptographic questions lie in the polynomial-factor regime.

importance.reason: A fundamental worst-case algorithm question at the heart of lattice reduction, with a wide gap between current methods and the target and connections to cryptographic hardness.

cards.status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. No classical polynomial-time algorithm with any fixed polynomial approximation factor was found for unrestricted Euclidean search SVP. Recent termination guarantees count costly subroutine calls, and the August conditional hardness theorem concerns constant factors. The card explicitly allows bounded-error classical randomization.

context_blocks.text: A lattice basis can disguise very short vectors as cancellations between long columns. For example, b₁=(N,1) and b₂=(N+1,1) both have length about N, while b₂−b₁=(1,0) has length one. Simply selecting the shortest input column therefore has no dimension-only approximation guarantee. Basis reduction changes the representation without changing the lattice, aiming to expose short integer combinations.

The LLL algorithm solves a major version of this task in polynomial bit time: with the standard reduction parameter, it finds a nonzero vector within 2^{(n−1)/2} of the shortest length. The factor is exponential in rank, even though the running time is polynomial. This was enough to transform computational number theory and enable applications such as factoring rational polynomials, but it leaves the much stronger approximation asked for here open.

Block reduction improves the quality by solving shorter-vector problems in projected sublattices of limited rank. The best general polynomial-time guarantees summarized by Bennett have approximation factor 2^{O(n log log n/log n)}. That is smaller than the basic LLL factor but still grows faster than every fixed power of n. Larger blocks improve approximation at the cost of more expensive local computations; a polynomial number of calls to an expensive subroutine does not imply polynomial total time.

Known hardness results approach, but do not reach, the polynomial-factor regime. Haviv and Regev show that approximation within 2^{(log n)^{1−δ}}, for fixed δ>0, cannot be polynomial time unless NP has randomized quasipolynomial-time algorithms. Stronger assumptions give further nearly polynomial factors. Every such factor must be read with its quantifiers: hardness for a smaller approximation factor concerns a more demanding task and does not eliminate the possibility of a much looser nᶜ approximation.

Decision and search also need care. GapSVP distinguishes λ₁≤r from λ₁>γr, with no requirement on intermediate inputs. Aharonov and Regev place the decision problem with γ=O(√n) in NP∩coNP, using short certificates on both sides. This is strong evidence about its structural complexity and a barrier to certain NP-hardness proofs. It is not a polynomial-time search algorithm that finds a short lattice vector.

The intermediate approximation regime is central to lattice cryptography. Worst-case to average-case reductions relate particular polynomial-factor lattice problems to problems such as SIS and LWE at specified parameters. These implications have a direction: an efficient worst-case algorithm would invalidate the corresponding hardness premise, but the existence of a security reduction alone would not prove that every deployed cryptosystem is broken. The exponent, problem variant and cryptographic parameters all matter.

Sato and Yasuda’s May 2026 PotBKZ algorithm guarantees termination after a polynomial number of calls to its potential-reducing enumeration routine. This improves control of the reduction process, including a self-dual variant. It does not give a polynomial-time polynomial-factor approximation for arbitrary rank, because the cost and quality of the block enumeration must still be accounted for.

Hirahara and Ogitsuka’s August 2026 preprint improves the randomness properties of lattice hardness reductions. Under a stated exponential lower-bound assumption for nondeterministic circuits, they obtain deterministic NP-hardness reductions for every constant Euclidean approximation factor. Both qualifications matter: the derandomization is conditional, and the approximation factors are constants, rather than all polynomial factors. Their separate parameterized hardness results also use a different resource measure.

The question isolates the large gap between useful reduction algorithms and the approximation range used in fundamental hardness assumptions. Even an algorithm with a very large fixed exponent C would be a major qualitative advance; the target does not demand exact SVP or a small approximation constant.

cards.title: The exact capacity region of the two-user Gaussian interference channel
cards.formal: Determine the capacity region C(a,b,P₁,P₂) of the memoryless real channel Y₁,t=X₁,t+aX₂,t+Z₁,t and Y₂,t=bX₁,t+X₂,t+Z₂,t for every fixed a,b∈ℝ and finite P₁,P₂≥0, with independent messages, average power constraints, no feedback or cooperation, and vanishing average decoding error. Equivalently, determine the exact function F(a,b,P₁,P₂,λ)=sup_{(R₁,R₂)∈C}[λR₁+(1−λ)R₂] for every λ∈[0,1], under the operational definitions below.
cards.definitions: For a block of n uses, messages M_i are independent and uniform on {1,…,K_{i,n}}. Transmitter i applies a deterministic encoder f_{i,n}:{1,…,K_{i,n}}→ℝⁿ depending only on its own message. Its codebook satisfies (nK_{i,n})⁻¹∑_{m=1}^{K_{i,n}}∑_{t=1}ⁿ f_{i,n}(m)_t²≤P_i. All Z_{i,t} are mutually independent N(0,1) random variables independent of the messages. Receiver i applies a measurable decoder g_{i,n}:ℝⁿ→{1,…,K_{i,n}} to its own received vector. The probability that either decoded message is wrong is averaged over both messages and all noise. A nonnegative pair (R₁,R₂) is achievable if there is a sequence of such codes with this error tending to zero and liminf_{n→∞} n⁻¹ log₂ K_{i,n}≥R_i for i=1,2. C is the closure of achievable pairs, measured in bits per real channel use. Gains, powers and both codebooks are known to all terminals. Arbitrary encoding across time and predetermined time sharing with power allocation are permitted; transmitters have no messages in common, output feedback, or communication between them. C is compact, convex and downward closed, so the nonnegative supporting function F uniquely determines it.
cards.answer_criterion: Formulation unfinished. The operational capacity region and supporting function are defined. The accepted finite-dimensional characterization has no specified syntax, allowed auxiliary distributions, dimension bound or evaluation requirement. Excluding a restatement informally is not a mathematical acceptance predicate; no new representation restriction is invented here.
cards.why: A defining problem in network information theory: even two interfering sender–receiver pairs expose limits of our ability to characterize optimal communication. An exact solution would distinguish which forms of message splitting, interference decoding and power allocation are fundamentally necessary.

importance.reason: A foundational multi-user capacity frontier with a simple channel model, strong approximate results and unresolved exact tradeoffs. Recent disputed claims make the precise formulation and status record especially valuable.

context_blocks.text: Two independent conversations share the same medium: each receiver sees its desired signal, a scaled version of the other sender’s signal, and Gaussian noise. With only one sender, Shannon’s formula gives the rate ½ log₂(1+P). With two senders, improving one link can make the other harder to decode. The mathematical object is therefore a two-dimensional region of feasible rate pairs. Knowing its largest total rate does not identify all tradeoffs between the users.

Han–Kobayashi coding splits each message into a part decoded by both receivers and a private part decoded only by its intended receiver. It includes treating interference as noise and decoding interference as special strategies. Time sharing can also allocate different powers to different phases while meeting the average constraints. Shang and Chen’s monograph organizes these inner bounds and the exact results in particular regimes, including the distinction between full regions and sum-rate capacity.

Strong interference is a solved benchmark. When |a|≥1 and |b|≥1, the capacity region consists of R₁≤½log₂(1+P₁), R₂≤½log₂(1+P₂), and R₁+R₂≤min{½log₂(1+P₁+a²P₂),½log₂(1+b²P₁+P₂)}. Both receivers can decode both messages. With a=b=0, the region is the rectangle given by the two individual bounds. These exact cases anchor the question but do not characterize arbitrary interference strengths.

Etkin, Tse and Wang show that a simple Han–Kobayashi strategy and new converse bounds locate the general region within a universal additive gap. Their celebrated one-bit theorem also gives high-signal-to-noise insights. A fixed gap can be extremely useful for system design while leaving the exact boundary unknown: it does not shrink merely because longer codes are allowed.

Recent work separates several different Gaussian-optimality questions. Nair and Zhao’s ISIT 2025 result identifies a substantial parameter range in the one-sided, or Z, channel where the optimized Gaussian-signaling region needs no multiplexing. This optimizes a particular achievable region; it does not prove that no other signaling distribution or coding strategy can do better.

Their January 2026 manuscript then shows that Gaussian distributions can be suboptimal within a single-phase Han–Kobayashi region when power control is disallowed. Its Conjecture 1 still asks whether Gaussian signaling with power control achieves full Z-channel capacity. Remark 2 reports difficulty verifying parts of an earlier Khandani proof claim. The counterexamples concern the restricted single-phase statement and do not disprove optimality after the allowed power allocation and time sharing.

Gohari, Nair and Zhao’s February 2026 work combines auxiliary-receiver and genie-aided converse techniques. Its Gaussian specialization captures known corner and sum-rate behavior, including associated changes in boundary slope. The theorem supplies an outer region rather than a general equality with an achievable region, so it advances the converse side without itself resolving the full target.

Khandani’s preprint, revised on 7 September 2026, makes a stronger claim: Gaussian Han–Kobayashi coding attains capacity throughout weak interference, with at most two time-sharing phases. This would settle a major part of the problem if established. The current revision has not been independently validated in this review. The earlier Nair–Zhao criticism predates it and cannot automatically be applied to every revised argument. This card therefore marks the present status as uncertain and records the claim explicitly.

The original short proposal cited a withdrawn paper by Huleihel and Merhav. Its claimed improvement using codewords with Gaussian memory was withdrawn in April 2018. Nair and Ng subsequently establish that temporally correlated Gaussian inputs do not enlarge the Gaussian Han–Kobayashi region once the comparison includes the appropriate scalar time sharing. The withdrawn result is retained only as a status correction, not as evidence of progress.

cards.title: The optimal asymptotic binary rate–distance tradeoff
cards.formal: Determine R₂(δ)=limsupₙ→∞ (1/n)log₂ A₂(n,⌈δn⌉) for every fixed real δ∈(0,1/2), where A₂(n,d) is the largest size of a binary length-n code with minimum Hamming distance at least d.
cards.definitions: A code C is any nonempty subset of {0,1}ⁿ; it need not be linear or efficiently encodable or decodable. The Hamming distance d_H(x,y) is the number of coordinates on which x and y differ. Require d_H(x,y)≥d for every pair of distinct codewords x,y∈C; a singleton satisfies this condition vacuously. A₂(n,d) is the maximum of |C| over all such subsets. A code has rate (log₂|C|)/n, measured in information bits per transmitted bit, and relative distance d/n. The ceiling fixes integer rounding. The limsup permits code families on a subsequence of blocklengths; existence of a full limit is not assumed. δ is fixed before n grows. All logarithms in this card are base two unless stated otherwise. The binary entropy function is h₂(t)=−t log₂t−(1−t)log₂(1−t), with 0 log₂0=0. The endpoint regimes are known: R₂(0)=1 and R₂(δ)=0 for 1/2≤δ≤1.
cards.answer_criterion: Formulation unfinished. The target R₂(δ) and equality conditions are defined, but an admissible answer representation is not. An arbitrary formula can just restate the defining optimization and limsup. A fixed representation or a separately approved proposition is still needed; replacing the question by tightness of a particular coding bound would change it.
cards.why: The basic unresolved packing limit for reliable binary information. An exact answer would identify how much redundancy is intrinsically necessary for a prescribed worst-case separation, independently of algorithmic or algebraic restrictions on the code.

context_blocks.text: A binary code represents messages by selected bit strings. Keeping codewords far apart lets a receiver distinguish them after errors, while selecting many codewords increases the amount of information carried by each transmitted block. The rate–distance function asks for the best possible compromise, allowing every conceivable code. It is therefore an information-theoretic limit that must be understood before asking how efficiently an optimal code can be built or decoded.

For a small example, the repetition code {000,111} has rate 1/3 and distance three, so it corrects one arbitrary flipped bit. The full set of eight three-bit strings has rate one and distance one, so it cannot correct even one arbitrary flip. Generally, disjoint Hamming balls of radius t around codewords are necessary and sufficient for unique correction of every pattern of at most t errors; this requires minimum distance at least 2t+1.

The Gilbert–Varshamov bound guarantees R₂(δ)≥1−h₂(δ). A maximal distance-d code covers the cube by balls of radius d−1, because otherwise another codeword could be inserted. Comparing the cube’s size with the volume of these balls gives the lower bound. In contrast, disjoint balls of radius roughly d/2 give the elementary Hamming upper bound 1−h₂(δ/2). The different radii create a genuine asymptotic gap.

McEliece, Rodemich, Rumsey and Welch’s 1977 linear-programming bounds greatly sharpen the converse. The first gives R₂(δ)≤h₂(1/2−√(δ(1−δ))); the second also uses constant-weight restrictions and is never weaker. The argument constrains a code’s distribution of pairwise distances through positivity relations, extracting information that a volume count loses. These were the long-standing general benchmarks, but they are no longer the strongest reported bounds after August 2026.

Alrabiah and Guruswami’s August 2026 preprint uses classical-input, quantum-output channels to prove stronger bounds for classical binary codes, including nonlinear codes. Mixed-qubit channels strictly improve the first MRRW bound, and a masked version strictly improves the second throughout 0<δ<1/2. Quantum states enter the converse proof as an analytical tool; the codes whose sizes are bounded still consist of ordinary bit strings. The result narrows the gap without matching the Gilbert–Varshamov lower curve.

Barg’s September 2026 note explains the relationship between this channel argument and a concurrent Delsarte-certificate proof. For the improvement of the first bound, he shows that the two variational expressions coincide. The geometric change is to associate a moving subspace, rather than a single vector, with each codeword, allowing a stronger packing argument. This provides a further derivation and interpretation of the new bound; it does not establish the exact rate function.

Lower-bound improvements require equally careful interpretation. Jiang and Vardy improve the finite-length Gilbert bound by a factor proportional to n in the fixed-distance regime they cover. Yuan and Zhu’s January 2026 preprint gives a concise probabilistic proof of a square-root-n improvement for linear codes and extends the method to quantum codes; the classical square-root factor had predecessors. After taking log₂ and dividing by n, any polynomial multiplicative factor contributes only O(log n/n). Such refinements do not increase the leading rate exponent.

Changing the error model also changes the answer. Capacity for independent random bit flips and capacity for list decoding are not the same quantity as the largest rate at a prescribed minimum distance. This card asks about worst-case pairwise separation with unrestricted binary codes. It also does not transfer improvements for sufficiently large alphabets directly to binary codes: changing alphabet and concatenating codes changes their rate and distance parameters.

cards.title: Effective classification of polynomially testable hereditary graph properties
cards.formal: Is there a total algorithm which, given a finite family F of finite simple graphs, decides whether induced-F-freeness admits a one-sided dense-model tester sampling at most C·ε^{−c} vertices, for some constants C,c depending only on F?
cards.definitions: The input to the classification algorithm is a finite list of adjacency matrices; the empty list is allowed. Let P_F contain exactly the finite simple graphs with no induced subgraph isomorphic to any member of F. For an n-vertex graph G, define dist(G,P_F) as the minimum number of edge additions or deletions needed to obtain a graph in P_F on the same vertex set, divided by n²; define the distance as +∞ when no such graph exists. For an integer s, the canonical tester chooses a uniformly random subset S of min{n,s} distinct vertices, queries all adjacencies in S, and rejects exactly when G[S] contains an induced member of F. Say that F is polynomially testable if there are integers C,c≥1 such that for every rational ε∈(0,1), every n≥1 and every G with dist(G,P_F)>ε, this tester with s=⌈Cε^{−c}⌉ rejects with probability at least 2/3. It automatically accepts every graph in P_F. The requested deterministic classification algorithm must halt on every finite F and answer YES exactly for these families. No runtime bound on that classification algorithm is imposed, and it need not output the constants C,c. Graph order n and accuracy ε are universally quantified in the property being classified; they are not additional inputs to the classification algorithm.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: Asks whether the efficient sampling regime of hereditary graph testing can be recognized from a finite description, turning a broad classification programme into a precise decidability target.

importance.reason: An effective formulation of the major finite-family classification problem; it separates polynomial sampling from mere testability and abstract quantitative equivalences.
